Multi-level marketing (MLM) is a marketing strategy in which the sales force is compensated not only for sales they personally generate, but also for the sales of the other salespeople that they recruit. This recruitment is meant to create a downline of distributors.
Salespeople are compensated in different ways. Most commonly, multi-level compensation takes the form of a binary compensation plan, where the salesperson is paid both on his or her personal sales, as well as a percentage of the sales made by the persons recruited into the sales force.
Multi-level marketing is controversial, and has been the subject of legal actions, in the United States and other countries, for alleged illegal pyramid schemes. It is also known as network marketing, by the participants, and has been the subject of much academic research.
The term “multi-level marketing” is often used in a broader sense than just the “binary compensation plan” described above. Other forms of multi-level marketing include the use of one-up and one-down concepts, where a product is sold only to consumers in the next higher level of the sales force, or the use of the product as a requirement for advancement in the sales force.

2005 was a landmark year for the legal and regulatory environment in which multi-level marketing companies operate. It began with a $27 million settlement by Amway to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) for alleged violations of the FTC’s 1979 amendments to the FTC Act and the FTC’s 1970 policy statement on multi-level marketing. This settlement, which was the largest ever by the FTC, was followed by the U.S. Senate Commerce Committee’s issuance of a report entitled “Urging Congress to Adopt Legislation Regarding the Federal Trade Commission and Multi-level Marketing,” and a letter to the FTC from Congresswoman Mary Bono requesting the FTC investigate whether Amway’s sales policies were illegal.
In January, the FTC announced it was conducting an investigation of multi-level marketing companies. This was followed in February with the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Connecticut bringing suit against a multi-level marketing company for violations of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act. The indictment included 11 counts of introducing unapproved new drugs into interstate commerce and one count of conspiracy to commit these offenses.
The Department of Justice issued a memorandum in February concerning the prosecution of corporate wrongdoing. This memo provides that the Department’s policy is to prosecute the individual responsible for the wrongdoing, rather than the corporation. It further provides that the Department will not recommend the entry of a non-prosecution agreement or a deferred prosecution agreement in the absence of a comprehensive plan to:
significantly enhance an organization’s compliance program;
terminate the misconduct at issue;
address the risks of future misconduct;
cause the organization to cooperate with the Department in its investigation; and
ensure that the organization is held accountable through meaningful remediation and appropriate punishment.

Mary Kay was also charged with mail fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit these offenses.

However, there are some companies that are more focused on recruiting people rather than selling product. These companies often use psychological tactics to persuade people to join their program, so they can then benefit from those people joining.
This is what makes MLM programs seem like a scam. However, if you look at it from a legitimate business point of view, it is not necessarily a scam.
As far as the psychological tactics are concerned, one of the key tactics used by MLM companies to get people to join is to use social proof.
Social proof is a psychological technique which uses other people as evidence to validate a product or service. If a lot of people are doing something, you are more likely to do it too.
Therefore, MLM companies will often show you a lot of people who have already joined their program. The psychology of social proof is so strong that you are more likely to want to join if other people are doing it.
One of the reasons why MLM companies have so much success in getting people to join is that it uses fear and threat.
Fear is a basic human emotion that can be used to get people to do things. If someone is saying, for example, that they are making lots of money and that you could be missing out, you are more likely to join in case you are missing out on something.
The fear is used as a threat – a threat that you might miss out, if you don’t join now.
The same thing happens when you are given an inflated sense of self-worth. This is when someone makes you feel good about yourself and tells you that you are a successful person, when you are not.
This is often done by comparing you to other people. It is known as the “comparative effect” and it is a psychological technique.
The idea is that when people are given an inflated sense of self-worth, they are more likely to believe it and want to protect their image by joining the program.
You might also be told that you are a loser if you don’t join, or that you might be a failure if you don’t join. You will then fear that you might be a failure, and so you will want to join in case you are a failure.
The key thing to note here is that MLM companies might make you feel good about yourself, and they might make you feel bad about yourself. This is all done to persuade you to join their program.

Most companies provide procedures for the handling of disputes and almost all companies have a participant code of conduct and an ombudsman.
The cost of handling complaints and disputes can be significant. Therefore, these companies are very careful to minimize disputes and to resolve them quickly.
Disputes are typically resolved internally within the company's system. If the dispute is not resolved within the system, then it can be escalated to the next level. For example, a distributor may take a dispute directly to the company and the company will investigate the matter and attempt to resolve it internally. If the dispute cannot be resolved by the company, then it can be escalated to the next level, usually the field leaders. If the dispute cannot be resolved by the field leaders, then it can be escalated to the next level, usually the corporate management.
Almost all companies have procedures and guidelines for the handling of disputes. For example, the Amway Code of Ethics is one such example.
It is common for a company to also have an "ombudsman", a person who is independent of the company and who has authority to handle disputes and provide arbitration. In some cases, the ombudsman is not paid by the company, but instead is paid by the participants themselves (usually by paying a small annual fee).
The process of handling disputes varies from company to company. In some cases, the company requires participants to resolve disputes internally before they can escalate the matter to the next level. When you buy from someone in the company, you make out a check to them. You must write the check to the sponsor not the company. Then the sponsor writes a check to the company and they pay the distributor.
When the company sends you a check, they send it to your sponsor. When the sponsor receives the check, they deposit it into their account. Once it is deposited, they write a check out to you and send it to you.
The sponsor does not make any money from these checks they simply keep track of them and pass them along to you.

This is where it gets a little tricky. The sponsor makes money when you sign up new people into their downline. This is done by simply showing you the ropes and teaching you how to sell the product.

Most MLM companies will put you through some type of training so that you can become a successful seller. They want you to be successful because they need you to be successful.

2018-10-18 As a multi-level marketing (MLM) distributor, you’re responsible for selling a product that you have no control over. And, like every other product sold in the United States, it could be recalled for any reason.
So how do MLM distributors handle product recalls and safety issues?
In our experience, distributors fall into three basic categories.
The first category is one that is not familiar with the product and does not know the product’s safety information. They are in the business of selling and are not concerned about the quality of the product. If the distributor is told of a recall, they may or may not heed the warning and continue selling the product.
The second category is one that is familiar with the product and does not know the product’s safety information. If the distributor is told of a recall, they may or may not heed the warning and continue selling the product.
The third category is one that is familiar with the product and knows the product’s safety information. If the distributor is told of a recall, they immediately remove the product from their inventory.
There is no “one size fits all” approach to this issue. The distributor’s response is dictated by the distributor’s knowledge of the product and the product’s safety information, their level of involvement in the business, their experience, and their desire to succeed.
There is no way for us to tell you which category you fall into. But we do want you to be aware that the industry has a history of distributors who were either not aware of a product’s recall or chose to ignore it.

4-5% of MLMs are pyramids, and the rest are legitimate MLMs.
There is no “magic number” to tell you which MLM is a pyramid and which one is a legitimate business. You can’t tell if you’re looking at a pyramid by the size of the compensation plan, the amount of products it offers, or the number of levels.
These are all red flags, but not indicative of a pyramid scheme.
To distinguish a pyramid scheme from an MLM, ask yourself three questions.
Do they sell legitimate products?
Are the compensation plans fair?
Do they have an established track record?
A pyramid scheme is defined by the FTC as a business model that “has no real product or service to offer consumers.
The company merely pays commissions for recruiting others to join and become salespeople.” It’s a scam because most people who join the company are more likely to lose money than make money.
Legitimate MLM companies have one or more products or services that are sold at retail prices.
In most cases, the products are akin to those sold by other companies. For example, Amway sells cleaning products, Pampered Chef sells kitchen gadgets, and Mary Kay sells cosmetics.
The products are not expensive, and they are sold at retail prices. In other words, you pay the same price for the product as anyone else who walks into a store.
This is a fairly easy question to answer because MLMs have compensation plans that are either flat-rate or multilevel. In the first case, the company pays you the same amount for every sale you make.
In the second case, the company pays you a percentage of what you sell to the customers you recruited. For example, if your sales team buys a product and then sells it to their customers, you would get a percentage of that sale.
The key thing to know is that both plans are fair. If one company is paying you flat-rate, they are paying the same percentage to everyone else on that level. The compensation plan is fair.
It’s not a pyramid scheme.
If they are fairly compensated and have an established track record, then you are dealing with an MLM.
If they are not fairly compensated and/or they don’t have an established track record, then you are dealing with a pyramid scheme.

10 years ago, multi-level marketing companies actively recruited minorities to form their own downlines. This was the best time to be a minority in MLM because the odds of them recruiting you were better. However, in the last 2-3 years, most companies have turned their focus to the non-minority market and it’s more difficult for minorities to get their foot in the door now. However, companies that still recruit minorities are most likely just not targeting the same minority communities anymore. The key is to find a company that’s still open to recruiting minorities.
Q: Can you name a few companies that are still open to minorities?
A: One company that comes to mind is AVON. They still do a great job at recruiting minorities. The problem is that AVON is still very focused on women. They have a very feminine image and that’s not very attractive to minority men. In addition, they have a lot of products that don’t really appeal to minority men. They’re not targeting men the way they should.
Also, there’s a lot of companies that are doing a better job of targeting minorities but they don’t have the same brand name recognition as the companies that are more established. One company that comes to mind is Isagenix. They’re a newer company and have a very strong emphasis on nutrition and weight management. A lot of minorities are interested in this and it’s a great opportunity for them.
Q: Why don’t minority MLM companies get as much publicity as the more well-known MLM companies?
A: One of the problems is that minority MLM companies don’t have as much marketing support. Most of the marketing support for MLM companies comes from the company. Many minority MLM companies don’t have the financial resources to promote themselves the way larger companies do. As a result, minority MLM companies have a much more difficult time getting their name out there and getting brand recognition.
Q: What advice do you have for minority MLM companies?
A: The number one thing that minority MLM companies need to do is develop a strong brand. You need to do everything in your power to make your company stand out from the rest. You can’t just be a fly by night company because you won’t be around for long. I know of a couple of minority companies that have a strong brand name but they’re not very aggressive. As a result, they’re not growing at the pace they should. When you have a strong brand name, people will flock to you.
Another thing minority MLM companies need to do is develop strong products. You need to have products that appeal to your target market. Minority MLM companies have a hard time because most of their products are geared towards women. You need to develop products that appeal to minority men as well as minority women.
The number three thing minority MLM companies need to do is hire a PR firm and a good marketing agency. You need to find people who are going to help you get your name out there. You can’t do it on your own. The people who are most successful have a team of experts behind them. You need to hire people who have connections in the media and know how to get your name out there. A PR firm can help you make your company stand out from the competition.
The last thing minority MLM companies need to do is work on their image. It’s all about perception. If you want to be successful, you need to be perceived as a legitimate company. You need to have your act together and be professionally run. You need to have a good website and make sure your products work.
Minority MLM companies have a lot of challenges. They face a lot of the same challenges as other MLM companies. The difference is that minority MLM companies face them at a greater degree. But, if you want to be successful, you need to work at it. If you want to be successful, you need to be willing to do what it takes to get your name out there. You can’t be a fly by night company. You need to develop a strong brand, develop strong products and hire people to get your name out there.

The recruiter gets a check from the company when a new recruit joins the program. If the recruiter is unable to recruit a new person, they will not get a check. This encourages recruiters to bring in as many recruits as possible.

Multi-level marketing,  also called network marketing, is a form of direct selling in which the salespeople are paid not only for the sales that they generate, but also for the sales of the people that they recruit. The structure of the business is such that the compensation of the salespeople is based on the sales of people they have recruited. This means that the salespeople must recruit many people in order to earn a substantial amount of compensation.
Multi-level marketing activities are governed by a host of regulations, depending on the country where they are operating.  This is because different countries have different legislative frameworks. The first issue that needs to be dealt with in the regulation of multi-level marketing is determining whether the company is engaged in a multi-level marketing activity or not.
An important distinction is to be made between multi-level marketing and pyramid selling. In pyramid selling, the participants make their money by joining the scheme and recruiting other people to join the scheme. In multi-level marketing, the participants make money by selling goods and/or services to customers and recruiting other salespeople to sell the goods and services. Multi-level marketing is a valid form of direct selling and is recognised in most countries.
The next issue is to determine the legal status of the company. Most countries have a number of legal entities which are recognised by the law and which are granted certain legal benefits. This includes, for example, the ability to enter into contracts and the ability to sue and be sued. There are also entities which are not recognised by law. This includes, for example, companies which are formed by a group of friends for the purpose of having fun, and companies which are formed by individuals for the purpose of participating in multi-level marketing activities.
Once the legal status of the company has been determined, the next issue is to determine the regulatory framework that applies. Different countries have different regulatory frameworks.
In some countries, multi-level marketing activities are subject to a specific law, such as the Direct Selling Association Act 2004 in Singapore. In other countries, the activities are regulated by a general law such as the Companies Act in Singapore. In still other countries, multi-level marketing activities are not subject to any law at all.
In addition to the laws that apply to multi-level marketing activities, there are other bodies of law that have a bearing on the activities. For example, the anti-pyramid selling laws will apply to multi-level marketing activities, where pyramid selling is involved.
The legal challenges that multi-level marketing companies face vary depending on the country in which they operate. In the Philippines, multi-level marketing companies are subject to the multi-level marketing law. In the United States, multi-level marketing companies are subject to the multi-level marketing laws and the anti-pyramid selling laws. In Singapore, multi-level marketing companies are subject to the multi-level marketing laws and the general laws such as the Direct Selling Association Act 2004 and the Unfair Trade Practices Act 1994.

15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(2)(A) requires the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to prevent unfair methods of competition and unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. To comply with this statute, the FTC has a number of administrative and judicial proceedings it may initiate against businesses. The FTC’s Telemarketing Sales Rule prohibits the deceptive use of endorsements and testimonials.
Multi-level marketing (MLM) programs are commonly used by small businesses to sell a variety of products, including cosmetics, health products, and nutritional supplements. In MLM programs, participants sell products to the public and recruit others to join the program, becoming participants themselves. The FTC has not identified any industry-wide problems with MLM programs, although the agency has seen individual instances of deception by some program participants.
FTC staff has not observed any industry-wide problems with MLM programs. If the agency became aware of a significant problem in this area, staff would conduct an investigation to determine if the problem warrants further action. The agency’s investigation would focus on whether deception, unfairness, or a violation of law occurred.
If the FTC discovers deceptive practices in an MLM program, it can take a variety of actions. First, the FTC may issue an administrative cease and desist order to stop the deceptive conduct. The FTC can also take action to stop the deceptive practices through the federal courts. For example, the FTC can file a civil lawsuit against the deceptive marketer to stop its practices. This action is known as a "prior restraint."
If the FTC finds that an MLM program is unfair, it can file a complaint against the marketer in federal court to stop the practice. If the court agrees with the FTC’s complaint, it can issue a cease and desist order and impose civil penalties of up to $16,000 per day against the company.
In addition, the FTC has authority to prevent the use of deceptive endorsements in advertising. The Telemarketing Sales Rule prohibits the deceptive use of endorsements and testimonials. 16 C.F.R. § 310.3(b). If the FTC finds that an MLM program is using endorsements deceptively, the agency can take action under the Telemarketing Sales Rule.
The FTC also has authority to bring actions under the Federal Trade Commission Act (FTC Act). The FTC Act prohibits deceptive practices that create a substantial probability of causing injury to consumers. 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(1). If the FTC finds that a marketer has engaged in deception that has caused substantial injury to consumers, it can bring an action against the company under the FTC Act. The action would include injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, and civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation.
If you have concerns about deceptive or unfair practices in MLM programs, please contact the FTC's Division of Consumer Protection.

2009 saw a string of lawsuits against multi-level marketing (MLM) companies that alleged that the companies’ compensation plans were too complicated and that they overstated the income earning potential of distributors. These suits included the following:
Class Action Lawsuit Against Sisel International, LLC
A class-action lawsuit against Sisel International, LLC, alleging that Sisel failed to disclose that a substantial portion of the income claimed by its distributors was from their enrollment in the company rather than from the sale of its products.
Class Action Lawsuit Against Herbalife International, Inc.
A class-action lawsuit against Herbalife International, Inc., alleging that Herbalife failed to disclose that a substantial portion of its distributors’ income was derived from the sale of products to other Herbalife distributors rather than from retail sales to customers.
Class Action Lawsuit Against Nu Skin Enterprises, Inc.
A class-action lawsuit against Nu Skin Enterprises, Inc., alleging that Nu Skin failed to disclose that a substantial portion of its distributors’ income was derived from the sale of products to other Nu Skin distributors rather than from retail sales to customers.
Class Action Lawsuit Against Usana Health Sciences, Inc.
A class-action lawsuit against Usana Health Sciences, Inc., alleging that Usana failed to disclose that a substantial portion of its distributors’ income was derived from the sale of products to other distributors rather than from retail sales to customers.
The allegations in these lawsuits focused on the compensation plans and income claims of the companies, rather than on the quality of the products. The suits are not the first of their kind, and they will not be the last. In each case, the plaintiffs alleged that the compensation plan, combined with the income claims, presented a false picture of the opportunities for participants. While the plaintiffs did not allege that the companies’ products were defective, the suits also alleged that the products were overpriced, and that the companies were engaged in deceptive and misleading marketing practices.

2018 was a difficult year for multi-level marketing companies (MLMs). In February, a class-action lawsuit against Herbalife Inc., alleging that it operated a pyramid scheme, was filed in a federal district court in Los Angeles. A pyramid scheme is a business model that recruits members by promising them a share of proceeds from a product or service sales of other recruits rather than by selling a product or service. In June, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced that it had reached a settlement with Herbalife. In addition to a $200 million refund, Herbalife agreed to make changes to its compensation plan. In August, Herbalife’s stock price was hammered by a report from Citron Research suggesting that the company could be exposed to a class action lawsuit due to the FTC settlement. The stock dropped 20 percent. By September, shares had fallen more than 50 percent from a high earlier that year.
Despite these developments, Herbalife’s multi-level marketing business model of selling vitamins and weight loss products has survived for 35 years. Herbalife is not alone; similar MLMs like Amway and Mary Kay have also been around for decades. What does it take for these businesses to be profitable? According to Forbes, Amway had revenues of $8.6 billion in 2018, with a net income of $702.1 million. The company has been profitable for three straight years. Mary Kay’s 2018 revenues were $3.6 billion, with a net income of $437.4 million. The company’s stock has increased by 50 percent since 2017.
Multi-level marketing companies, also referred to as direct selling or network marketing companies, have been around since the 1950s. The business model involves a pyramid-shaped structure, with a small number of people at the top earning a large amount of money, while the vast majority of people are at the bottom earning a small amount of money. The MLM structure is different from a traditional marketing model, where the majority of customers buy products directly from the company. They may also claim that the product is a fad, or that there is a shortage of the product, or that the product will be taken off the market soon. ​The “culture” of multi-level marketing companies is different from that of other businesses, and sometimes it is difficult for an outside observer to understand what is going on in the company. Some MLM companies and lawyers will suggest that it is best to have an “arm’s-length” relationship between the company and participants in order to avoid issues of improper influence and undue influence. This means that the participants should be self-motivated to do what is required to build their business, and should not be relying on promises by company officials or co-workers.
One thing that makes it difficult for an outside observer to understand what is going on in a MLM company is that the company is usually a small business and participants may be employed by the company or some other person or entity. So the person who is in charge of the company may also be the person who is supposed to be providing the necessary training and compliance guidance. This creates an obvious conflict of interest, and if the company is not transparent about the compliance requirements, it is difficult to avoid miscommunication and misinterpretation of what is expected of a participant.
Because of this conflict, some MLM companies have created a formal system for participants to report compliance issues, which they can use to report concerns to an internal “investigative team” and/or to outside government agencies. In some cases, the company has a policy of not retaliating against the participant who reports a compliance problem, and, where necessary, the company will remove the offending participant from the company. The company will also sometimes take action against the participant who violates the policies and procedures.
The problem with this approach is that the company does not always have a system that is foolproof. The company will not always follow up on the issues reported, or the company may be more interested in avoiding public scrutiny and not wanting to admit that there is a problem. If the company does not take necessary action, the government will typically get involved, and this may affect the company’s reputation and, in extreme cases, may affect the company’s ability to continue operating.
So, it is a difficult situation for a multi-level marketing company, and, in my experience, the best approach is to have a system where the company has policies and procedures that are easily accessible and that are enforced. For example, the company should have a written set of policies and procedures that are specific to MLM, and this should be available on the company’s website. In addition, the company should have a procedure for reporting compliance issues, and this procedure should be known and made available to all participants. The company should have a procedure for taking appropriate action when a compliance issue is reported, and this procedure should be known and made available to all participants.
This does not mean that a company should not use personal relationships to provide motivation to participate, and it does not mean that there should be no cooperation among participants, but it does mean that the company should have a transparent system that allows participants to know what they need to do to avoid violating the policies and procedures of the company.

You can see why it’s so difficult to ever truly know the motives of the users of online media, because there are so many techniques to conceal identity. In the case of the Asch experiment, however, the method of covertly manipulating the subjects’ behaviors could not be used, because the participants knew that their performance was being evaluated. It would be much more difficult to manipulate the behaviors of people on an anonymous message board or chat room, for instance, where it would be extremely difficult to obtain any objective data about their actual performances. The use of covert manipulation, or baiting, as it’s sometimes called, could, however, be done in the case of someone who is being paid to comment on a product or service. A blogger might be paid to write about how much he loves a certain brand of toothpaste, and could be told that the comments will be made anonymously, so that he can speak freely, but in reality, the comments could be manipulated to appear as if he really loves the toothpaste. And there are a lot of people who would be happy to do this kind of work, and they do it for very little pay, even when they have to hide their real identities.
Designers are now using techniques to determine if a user is a robot or a person.
Most online marketers would argue that some of the above techniques are used in this industry as well, and there are probably some truth to it, but I’m sure it’s far more subtle than what’s described above.
In the end, there’s no way to truly know how, or what, someone writes on an online message board, and it’s frustrating, because it’s so difficult to determine who is telling the truth and who is lying.
The best thing to do, in my opinion, is to rely on the facts, and not the emotions that are invoked by heated arguments. In my opinion, the most effective tool for doing this is a good logical argument. But it’s really up to the readers to do their homework, and to use their judgment to determine what is true, and what isn’t.

2015’s amendment to the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA) removed FDA regulation of most products that claim to be dietary supplements, including those marketed for weight loss, sexual enhancement, and detoxification. While dietary supplements are not drugs, they are often promoted as such, without restrictions or regulation. For example, the manufacturer of OxyElite Pro, a product marketed as a dietary supplement, was ordered to halt production after it was linked to 13 deaths and 1,400 reports of liver damage.
In general, manufacturers are not required to get FDA approval before marketing a new dietary supplement. And the dietary supplement industry is not subject to the same safety requirements as conventional drug companies. Dietary supplements do not have to be proven safe and effective before they reach the market. Manufacturers can claim that their products are safer, more effective, or better than any other product if they have “substantial evidence” to back up their claims, but the FDA does not regulate these claims. Dietary supplement manufacturers can make a wide variety of claims about their products, including that they can prevent, treat, or cure diseases.
Dietary supplement manufacturers are not required to report adverse events to the FDA. However, manufacturers are required to include a “black box” warning on the label of their products. A black box warning is the FDA’s strongest warning, used when the FDA considers a product to be dangerous. The black box warning on the label of OxyElite Pro, for example, states that it should not be taken by individuals with heart disease, high blood pressure, or liver disease, and that it may cause liver damage.
The FDA has the authority to take action when a dietary supplement is harmful or is misbranded or adulterated. The FDA can issue a warning letter to manufacturers, seize products that are misbranded or adulterated, and, in rare cases, seek an injunction to prevent the distribution of a harmful product. In 2012, the FDA took steps to require some dietary supplement manufacturers to submit evidence that their products were safe and effective before marketing them. But a federal court ruled that the FDA’s requirements did not go far enough to protect consumers and overturned the regulations.
Although the FDA is legally unable to restrict claims made by dietary supplement manufacturers, it can encourage manufacturers to provide information about the risks associated with their products. If you believe that you have been harmed by a dietary supplement, it is a good idea to contact a lawyer to discuss your options for filing a lawsuit.
For information on dietary supplements, see What Every Consumer Should Know About Dietary Supplements (from the FDA) and Understanding Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (from the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health).

The good news is that mobile banking fraud is highly preventable.
Mobile banking apps are a great way to pay bills and transfer money between accounts, but they do have a few weaknesses.
Here, we take a look at the main ones, so you can make sure you stay safe.
What are the weak spots?
Mobile apps are easy to access, so scammers can easily steal your credentials if you don’t take proper precautions.
Even if you think you’re being careful, you could still fall for a phishing scam, where you’re tricked into entering your online banking login details on a fake website, which looks like the real thing.
The most important thing to do is always make sure you’re on the official website.
If you’re not sure, there should be a link on the app that leads to the official site.
Another thing to bear in mind is that the longer you spend on the mobile banking app, the more the risk of fraud increases.
As soon as you’ve completed a transaction, it’s vital that you log out properly and close the app.
If you fail to do this, scammers can continue to use your login details to access your account, and do further damage to your bank balance.
How can I stay safe?
The most important thing is to be careful when you’re using your mobile banking app.
Take a look at the top tips below, so you know exactly what to do to stay safe.
- Make sure you always use your mobile banking app on the official website
- Be wary of any suspicious emails, texts or calls
- Always log out properly, and close the app
- Don’t install any apps from unknown sources
- Keep your phone and computer up to date
- Use an app with a PIN or fingerprint login
If you think you’ve already been a victim of mobile banking fraud, you should contact your bank and creditors immediately.

Q: What are the elements of insider trading?
A: The following elements must be present to demonstrate insider trading: (1) a fiduciary relationship, (2) a disclosure of confidential information, (3) the violation of a duty, and (4) a resulting misappropriation.
1. Fiduciary Relationship
The first element requires a fiduciary relationship to exist between the insider and the investor. It is important to note that the insider-investor relationship does not have to be a formal arrangement, such as a contract or employment agreement. For example, if one person is the sole trustee of a trust with assets in excess of $5,000,000, and he makes a disclosure to the investor, he will have a fiduciary relationship with the investor.
Fiduciary relationships can also be implied. In implied fiduciary relationships, the insider has the primary responsibility to protect the investor's interests. A fiduciary relationship will exist if an insider in a relationship of trust, confidence, or special skill in the investor. A fiduciary relationship also exists when an insider in a position of authority over an investor makes a disclosure to the investor. An example of an implied relationship is an attorney providing legal advice to a client.
The second element requires the insider to make a disclosure of confidential information to the investor. For the insider to have committed insider trading, the information must be of a nonpublic character. Nonpublic information is information that is not available to the general public. For example, information about a company's merger plans is not considered public information unless the company has released the information to the public.
3. Violation of a Duty
The third element requires the insider to violate a duty, breach the trust, or act in a way that conflicts with the insider's fiduciary duties. The insider must have used the confidential information to make a decision about when to purchase or sell a security. The insider must have done this while the information was not available to the general public.
4. Misappropriation
The fourth element requires a misappropriation of the confidential information. The misappropriation must be illegal or improper. If the insider uses the information to purchase or sell a security, he or she is considered to have misappropriated the information.
Q: When can an insider trade and when is that illegal?
A: Insider trading is legal if the insider is following his or her duty to the investor and is acting in the investor's best interest. Insider trading is illegal if the insider violates his or her fiduciary duty to the investor by trading on the basis of the confidential information.

4chan is a collection of anonymous user forums, and while a lot of the content of the forums are legitimate discussions and the like, it does feature a lot of posts and images depicting self-harm and abuse. The site's rules prohibit posting links to such material, but there are a large number of threads dedicated to documenting and sharing such content. Most of the activity in such threads is composed of people expressing outrage that such a thing could happen, but a very small number of the forum participants are genuinely encouraging self-harm and abuse.
While the discussions are often just people venting their frustration at the concept of someone posting such material and the idea that people should be able to post such material anonymously, it is not uncommon for a thread to get started by someone specifically encouraging self-harm.
There are also forums for people who self-harm, but because they are forums on which people can post anonymously, they are often populated by people who are looking for other people to self-harm with them or are simply encouraging one another in their habit of self-harm. While it isn't uncommon for people who self-harm to seek out other people who self-harm in an attempt to find a group that will understand and support their actions, the self-harm communities on the internet are not safe places for those with self-harm tendencies to seek out support. The support they offer is almost always an illusion, and the actual support that does exist can be difficult to find as most of the forum activity is centered around encouraging self-harm.
Sometimes people with self-harm tendencies do seek out communities like this one, and while this site is not a support forum, we are happy to offer support to those who have self-harmed and are seeking to stop. If you are seeking help with self-harm, please visit this page to see if there is a support forum available in your area.

99% of online platforms are built on one simple principle: to connect people. The fact that this connection is made through an online platform, and with the support of a community of people, is often a key element to feeling less lonely and to feeling more supported. The role of the community and the platform to promote positive outcomes is of fundamental importance.
Platforms tend to play two roles: a) to facilitate self-expression, and b) to moderate or remove harmful content. The first role is generally based on the idea of ‘freedom of expression’, while the second is based on the idea of ‘freedom from harm’.
In general, platforms tend to make a distinction between the two roles, and they tend to develop tools and processes to handle each of the roles differently.
On the one hand, platforms tend to develop tools and processes to provide moderation and removal for harmful content. For example, if a suicide note is published on a platform, the platform will remove that post and could take down the user’s account as well.
On the other hand, platforms tend to develop tools and processes to enable users to express themselves. For example, they will provide users with mechanisms to flag a post, or to prevent the post from being seen by others.
This distinction is not always 100% clear, and it is not always perfectly separated in practice.
It is also important to note that there is no single global approach to self-expression and the removal of harmful content. Platforms tend to adapt their approaches and tools to their local contexts.
What this means for the self-harm and suicide community is that, while the idea of a platform having a clear role in promoting a positive outcome is the general approach, the application of this principle will vary across different platforms.
In other words, we believe that suicide and self-harm prevention tools should be made available to all platforms, and that all platforms should adhere to a set of principles in this respect. This will allow for the creation of a shared ecosystem that can help millions of people, and that will also help to bridge the digital divide.
At the same time, it is important to acknowledge that the way platforms are built, and the way they are used, will shape how the principle of a ‘clear role in promoting a positive outcome’ will be applied.
When it comes to the moderation of harmful content, platforms will typically ask themselves: a) what is the harm?, b) who is the harm for?, and c) how much harm is this?
The answer to the first question, ‘what is the harm?’, will determine whether a post is considered to be harmful.
As an example, if a post is considered to be a suicide note, then it is likely to be considered harmful. The harm in this case would be for the person who wrote the note, and the harm would be a lot of harm.
The answer to the second question, ‘who is the harm for?’, will determine the profile of the user that is targeted by the moderation.
As an example, if a post is considered to be a suicide note, and if it is considered to be harmful, then it is likely to be moderated or removed from the platform if it is for the benefit of the person who wrote the note.
The answer to the third question, ‘how much harm is this?’, will determine the extent of the moderation.
As an example, if a post is considered to be a suicide note, and if it is considered to be harmful, then it is likely to be moderated or removed from the platform if it is for the benefit of the person who wrote the note. However, if it is not for the benefit of the person who wrote the note, then it is likely to be moderated or removed from the platform to a lesser extent.
Note: the answers to the three questions will vary depending on the type of harmful content being moderated.
In general, the following rules tend to apply:
a) platforms will moderate content with the aim of preventing harm.
b) platforms will moderate content that is deemed to be harmful.
c) platforms will moderate content for the benefit of the person who is targeted by the content.
d) platforms will moderate content to a lesser extent for the benefit of others.
There are, however, exceptions to these rules. In some cases, platforms will moderate content for the benefit of others, and will not moderate for the benefit of the person who is targeted by the content.

2015 research has shown that viewing graphic images of self-harm can make a person more emotionally sensitive to future self-harm images. This effect also increases with the number of images viewed. Additionally, the research suggests that the empathetic response to these images is still present even when the person is not displaying self-harm behaviors. This research challenges the notion that viewing graphic images of self-harm can desensitize the viewer and calls for a more nuanced understanding of how this exposure may influence behavior.

​Depictions of self-harm in movies and TV shows often show a character cutting or stabbing themselves. These are very graphic images and can be extremely upsetting to those who have or are considering self-harming. Many people argue that this kind of imagery normalizes self-harm behavior and glamorizes it.
Because these images are so prevalent in media, they may affect the behavior of those who are vulnerable to self-harm. In fact, some self-harmers may be more likely to try self-harm as a result of seeing it in films and TV shows. That’s why it’s important for parents to be aware of what their kids are watching and to make sure that they are not glamorizing self-harm behavior through their media choices.
For these reasons, many movies and TV shows have tried to avoid depicting self-harm. It’s also important to note that there are ratings for films and TV shows that are designed to help parents understand how violent content is presented and how graphic it may be. The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) and the Television Parental Guidelines can help parents understand the nature and extent of the violence in the movies and TV shows that their children watch.
It’s important to note that movies and TV shows are not always very realistic and that what they depict is often exaggerated for dramatic effect. In most cases, self-harm is not depicted in a positive light and it’s likely that the intent of the movie or TV show is to discourage it.

Q: What is the relationship between eating disorders and binge eating?
A: Although all eating disorders involve the misperception of body weight and/or shape, binge eating disorder (BED) is the most common eating disorder in the United States. It’s a type of eating disorder marked by recurring episodes of binge eating, but not purging, fasting, or excessive exercise.
Q: How is eating disorder recovery measured?
A: Long-term studies have shown that 50% to 60% of individuals who are treated for eating disorders recover completely and do not have symptoms a year after treatment.
Q: What are the most common signs of an eating disorder?
A: Eating disorders can have a variety of signs and symptoms, including changes in eating behaviors, a preoccupation with food and weight, and a significant drop in weight.
Q: Is there a genetic link to eating disorders?
A: There is evidence that genetics may play a role in the development of eating disorders. The likelihood of developing an eating disorder increases if a close relative has one.
Q: Are eating disorders more common in women?
A: Eating disorders are most common in young women, and they are twice as common in women as in men.
Q: Are there other risk factors for eating disorders?
A: There are many risk factors for eating disorders, including: stress, low self-esteem, poor body image, a history of trauma, a history of abuse, and a family history of eating disorders.

2019 has been an unprecedented year for cyber attacks. The latest attack on the Houston Ship Channel—the busiest port in the United States and the second busiest port in the world—is a stark reminder of the potential impacts of a cyber attack on critical infrastructure in the water sector.
The Texas A&M University Transportation Institute (TTI) helps water utilities and other infrastructure owners and operators develop and implement resilience plans to ensure that they are prepared for the worst.
TTI is a leader in the water sector. For more than 50 years, TTI has developed innovative solutions to help water utilities solve challenges related to floods, water security, water quality, water loss, wastewater treatment, and more.
TTI’s resilience efforts include a variety of activities:
Partnerships: TTI is collaborating with water utilities, state and local governments, academic institutions, and other organizations on various resilience-related efforts. Recent efforts include Texas Water Resilience Collaborative (TWRC), a statewide collaboration to help the Texas water sector build resilience; and Texas Resilient Communities Project (TRCP), a TTI effort that helps communities across Texas strengthen their resilience to disasters.
Training: TTI has a long track record of training water professionals, including the State of Texas Leadership Program (STLP)—the first water sector leadership program in the nation. TTI also has developed training programs to help water professionals better understand resilience and resilient design. Recent training efforts include the Texas Stormwater Training Program (TSTP), a statewide training program for the Texas stormwater industry; and the Center for Resilient Infrastructure Research and Education (CRIRE), a TTI effort to help ensure the safety, security, and sustainability of water and other infrastructure.
Research and development: TTI has a long track record of research and development activities in the water sector. Recent examples include development of an innovative sensor and software that can detect microbes in drinking water and a system that uses recycled water for fire suppression.
TTI is helping ensure that the water sector is resilient. Find out more about TTI’s water sector resilience efforts by contacting Dr. Thomas Edgar.

​The Chinese government has for decades been successful in penetrating other countries’ computer networks and pilfering their secrets, from industrial technology to military capabilities, and now it has its sights on a new target: the United States.
Chinese hackers have systematically stolen information from the U.S. defense industry, technology companies and government agencies, according to U.S. intelligence officials and outside experts. The targeting has intensified in recent years as the Chinese have become more aggressive and their spies have grown more skilled.
The spying has accelerated to such an extent that the Obama administration is considering a range of possible responses, including economic sanctions and other actions that could force Beijing to change its behavior.
Nation-states have been stealing secrets from each other for centuries, but the sheer volume of data being stolen now is unprecedented, U.S. officials said. Foreign espionage is nothing new, they added, but the theft of intellectual property is on a scale and with a sophistication that experts say is unmatched.
“It’s a game changer,” said James Lewis, a former Commerce Department official who is now a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “You’ve got to change your model of how you do business and how you protect your assets.”
The U.S. government has been warning companies and the private sector for years of this growing threat. Chinese companies have been implicated in some of the most brazen cases, including the 2010 breach of Google Inc.’s computer network.
Yet the level of attacks appears to have increased and the targeting has become more sophisticated, according to U.S. officials and outside experts.
“This is the most sustained, the most voracious, the most wide-scale, the most damaging and the most costly” form of industrial espionage in the U.S., said James A. Lewis, the CSIS analyst. “It’s unprecedented.”
U.S. officials say Chinese hackers are the most prolific perpetrators, but the thieves are not necessarily working for China’s government. Chinese-run companies have also been implicated in some cases, and many of the attacks appear to be the work of criminal syndicates.
But the government is widely believed to be directing the hacking efforts, and the involvement of criminal groups is thought to be a tactic to help deflect attention.
It isn’t easy to trace the thefts back to their sources. Chinese hackers often are able to break into networks of foreign companies and then quietly steal information from inside the networks, sometimes for months or years, with few or no signs of intrusion.
“Chinese spies are engaged in a robust and pervasive campaign of cyber espionage against all sectors of our economy,” Derek Manky, chief information security officer at Fortinet, a cyber-security firm, said in testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee. “In some cases, they are stealing entire companies’ intellectual property.”
The potential economic consequences are huge. For instance, the theft of design and manufacturing secrets could cost the U.S. aerospace industry more than $600 billion over the next 20 years, according to an estimate from the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments.
The costs would be higher still if China were to reverse-engineer stolen U.S. technology and then begin to manufacture it itself, said Richard Fisher, a senior fellow at the International Assn. of Intelligence Services.
“The biggest damage would be not just the loss of intellectual property but the loss of technology, and the loss of technology would be the loss of jobs,” Fisher said. “It would be a huge hit.”

18 U.S.C. § 2257(a)(1)(A)
18 U.S.C. § 2257(a)(1)(A) requires the following:
(A) if the producer or other person responsible for such display or publication does not have actual knowledge that the matter depicted therein is unlawful under this chapter;
The courts have interpreted this provision to mean that the producer must be unaware that the content may be obscene, so that would include graphic material that depicts self-harm or suicide. In the case of United States v. Wade, 523 F.Supp. 865 (N.D. Cal. 1981), for example, the court ruled that "the actor cannot be deemed to have had actual knowledge of the obscenity of the underlying material, simply because that material is depicted in the context of an explicit sex act."
In the case of United States v. Anderson, 589 F.Supp. 131 (N.D. Ga. 1984), the court found that the producer was not aware that the material had any connection to actual child pornography, and ruled that § 2257(a)(1)(A) could not be applied to such an unknowing producer.
The case of United States v. Wade, 543 F.Supp. 984 (N.D. Cal. 1982), also involved a prosecution of a producer for obscenity for using graphic material of self-harm, but the court determined that the producer did have actual knowledge of the material's obscenity and dismissed the case.

18 U.S.C. § 876, commonly known as the “Bridgeghazi” statute, prohibits transmitting in interstate or foreign commerce any communication containing a threat to injure the person of the President of the United States or other person authorized to hold that office, or the spouse, child, or parent of any such person, with intent to place the person in fear of death or bodily harm.
It is a federal crime to intentionally threaten the President or other authorized high-level government officials with violence. According to the law, the threat must be “a knowing and willful” effort to terrorize or intimidate the President or other official. For instance, threatening the President by bombing a bridge is a violation of the statute, but threatening him by bombing a bridge without naming the President is not. The statute applies to any communication that is transmitted in interstate or foreign commerce. In 2008, the Supreme Court ruled that the statute also applies to communications transmitted over the Internet.
Individuals who are convicted under this statute face a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

This is a question that has many facets. And since it is a question of law, it depends on the law in the jurisdiction in question.
The general principles are that you are not legally allowed to lie about someone. You are not allowed to libel someone (that is, you cannot say something about someone that is untrue, and that is damaging to their reputation).
However, you are not legally obliged to say something that you know is untrue, nor are you legally obliged to not say something you know is true.
This means that you can say that you know something is untrue and not be liable for libel.
However, this is not a general principle. For example, in the United States you have a Constitutional right to free speech. But that right is not absolute.
You can still be held liable for libel. And you can be sued.
The courts in the United States have, over time, found that there is a difference between, say, saying "I know that Joe is a homosexual," and saying "Joe is a homosexual." The courts have found that the second statement is libelous, but the first statement is not.
In general, then, you can say things about someone that are untrue. And that you know are untrue. But if you say them in such a way that people will likely take them as fact, you can be held liable for libel.
But there is more to it than that.
If you make a statement that is untrue, and you later discover that it is true, you can be sued for libel, too. And you can be held liable for libel.
If you make a statement that is true, and you later discover that it is false, you can be sued for libel, too. And you can be held liable for libel.
And, of course, there are other situations where you can be held liable for libel, even if you are not intentionally making a libelous statement. For example, if you say something that is true, but that you knew or should have known was untrue.

1. As a general rule, the most common legal issues that individuals have with free speech are (a) time, place and manner restrictions, (b) disorderly conduct laws, and (c) defamation claims.
(a) Time, place and manner restrictions: Time, place and manner restrictions can be seen as a matter of law and order. In other words, the government can restrict what you can say in a public place. Public places include parks, streets, sidewalks, and other government-owned property. Private property can also be restricted, but only with the consent of the owner of the property.
Most time, place and manner restrictions are content-neutral. For example, you cannot scream "FIRE" in a crowded theater and cause a panic. It does not matter if your message is or is not true. You cannot commit an act of false flag terrorism and then claim that your free speech rights were violated by a time, place, and manner restriction.
(b) Disorderly conduct laws: Disorderly conduct laws are also aimed at the time, place, and manner of speech. However, disorderly conduct laws are more concerned with how you act than what you say.
If you make a nuisance of yourself by yelling obscenities, even if your message is valid, you may be cited for disorderly conduct. Therefore, it is a good idea to have a reasonable, but clear, message.
(c) Defamation claims: Defamation is a claim for false and damaging statements. Defamation is the only type of speech that is recognized as a right by the First Amendment.
A defamation claim must meet three criteria: (1) a statement of fact; (2) negligence; and (3) harm. A statement of fact is a statement that is either true or false. However, a statement of fact can be false even if it is true. For example, if a person claims that you are a pedophile, you could sue for defamation if the statement is false. However, you could not sue for defamation if you really are a pedophile.
The burden of proof is on the plaintiff. The plaintiff must prove the statement is false by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).
Negligence refers to the negligent conduct of the person who made the statement. Negligence refers to the carelessness of the person who made the statement. For example, the person who made the statement must have known that the statement was false.
Finally, the statement must have caused harm. The statement must have caused harm to your reputation or business. It is not enough to simply feel offended by the statement.
Some defamation claims are allowed. For example, a defamation claim for negligent infliction of emotional distress is allowed. In other words, if someone makes a false statement that causes you to suffer emotional distress, you can sue for defamation.
Hate speech and defamation are two different things. Hate speech is protected by the First Amendment. However, defamation claims are allowed and recognized by the First Amendment.

This family of malware was reportedly the first malware that targeted UK users exclusively. It also targeted users in Germany and France, and featured a downloader designed to infect the victim’s PC and load the malware onto it, as well as a web browser exploit to infect the user’s PC.
The Crimson Snifter malware is designed to steal credit card numbers and other sensitive information, as well as gather information from the victim’s computer.
Another example of this is the Targeted Access Trojan, which is designed to infect government computers. One of its features includes the ability to launch commands and run applications, while also being able to change the language of the operating system.
The Targeted Access Trojan was created by a group known as Hacking Team, which was a hacker group that was caught last year when a cache of the group’s information was leaked to the public. Hacking Team was a company that created advanced surveillance software for governments. It was eventually revealed that the company was selling its products to governments in Morocco, Egypt, Panama, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Kazakhstan, Thailand, Mexico, Colombia, and Malaysia.

The central questions here are (1) whether a machine-learning-based system can be devised that is sufficiently strong to counter malware, and (2) whether it is possible for a malware author to circumvent the detection logic of such a system. The answer to (1) is a qualified "yes." The answer to (2) is "yes, but not for long."
Let's start with the "yes" on (1). If machine-learning-based malware detection is based on a generalization of the P vs. NP problem -- that is, if it is based on using a Bayesian network to represent the probability that a file is malware given its attributes -- then a malware author can evade detection by deliberately crafting malware to have attributes that are more likely to be benign than those of a file that is malware. For example, a malware author could craft a file that is large, because files that are large are more likely to be benign than those that are small. However, there are two limitations to this approach. First, it would be impossible to craft a file that is large enough to be more likely to be benign than malware. Second, in most cases, it would be impossible to craft a file with the attributes that are more likely to be benign than malware. The reason is that this would require the malware author to be able to predict future changes in the attributes of malware -- something that is impossible.
This type of attack requires that the malware author be able to know the current (and thus, the future) attributes of malware. However, this is not the only way that malware can evade machine-learning-based detection. The most common way is the same way that malware evaades all other forms of detection: obfuscation. The malware author simply obfuscates the malware so that the machine-learning-based system is unable to detect it. This is typically done by encrypting the malware or by encoding it in a different format.
The answer to (2) is "yes, but not for long." First, malware authors are highly creative, and a machine-learning-based malware detection system will be no more effective than a conventional one. Second, machine-learning-based malware detection systems can be trained to detect malware that has been obfuscated. The technique is to use a larger corpus of malware to train the system. After the system has been trained, it is applied to the malware and then compared to the result of running it through the machine-learning-based malware detection system without training. If the system is better than the conventional system, then the malware author can use the obfuscated malware to train a machine-learning-based system to detect it.

A common social engineering trick is to use "industry jargon." They may use words such as antivirus, spyware or firewalls to trick a user into thinking that they're talking to a legitimate company or technician. Once the user is duped, the scammer will then ask to remotely take over the computer.
2. Using Fake Programs
Another common technique involves using fake programs. For example, a scammer may pretend to be a legitimate program publisher such as Microsoft, Apple or Symantec and offer to send the user a new program. Of course, the program that the user actually receives isn't legitimate. Once the user is tricked into installing the malware, the scammer will then ask to remotely take over the computer.
3. Using Pop-Ups
Most scammers use some type of pop-up to try to trick users into thinking they're communicating with a legitimate company. In fact, scammers use pop-ups for all sorts of different tricks.
4. Using Fake Website Links
Another technique involves using fake website links. Scammers may place ads on websites with legitimate-sounding names such as "AOL Security Toolbar" or "Trend Micro Scan and Clean." The ads will usually contain some type of interesting information such as an alert about a virus or the need to update your security software. Once the user is tricked into clicking on the ad, the scammer will then ask to remotely take over the computer.
5. Using Browser Toolbars
Another tactic is to try to get users to install a browser toolbar. Many legitimate browser toolbars provide useful features such as the ability to block pop-up ads or add additional search options.
However, scammers often use browser toolbars to try to trick users into installing malware. Once installed, the scammer will ask to remotely take over the computer.
6. Using Fake Spyware or Adware Removal Tools
Sometimes scammers will pretend to be an antivirus company such as Norton or McAfee. They'll then claim that your computer is infected with spyware, adware or a virus and offer to sell you a spyware removal tool. The scammer will then try to trick the user into installing the tool. However, in reality, the tool that the user actually installs is malware.
7. Using Social Networking

For example, malware is designed to steal money from your bank account and from your PayPal account. Malware is also designed to steal money from you by accessing your credit cards and personal information.
For years, the anti-malware industry has said that it is not possible to design malware that can evade detection. That statement is now proven to be wrong. The statement is wrong because malware authors have been able to evade detection, and because behavioral analysis-based security solutions are, by nature, not able to detect 100% of malware.
The problem with the statement is that it implies that malware authors will not be able to evade detection. That is a false statement. The only way that malware authors will not be able to evade detection is if behavioral analysis-based security solutions are able to detect 100% of malware. Unfortunately, that is not the case. Behavioral analysis-based security solutions are designed to detect 99.999% of malware.
In a perfect world, all malware would be detected by a behavioral analysis-based security solution. That is not the case, and it never will be the case. Malware authors will continuously design new malware to evade detection.
The only way to protect against malware is to use a solution that has a 100% detection rate. The only solution that has a 100% detection rate is a physical disk with 100% backups.
So, no. Malware can be designed to evade detection by behavioral analysis-based security solutions.

provision, parties and campaigns are permitted to use artificial

is the Communications Decency Act of 1996, which governs the use of
computers in the dissemination of certain types of information, such as
commercial speech and other information that involves political
speech.  However, most political parties and campaigns are not covered
by the statute and, as a result, have no obligation to obtain the
necessary licenses or permits to use computers.

with artificial intelligence?

apply to the use of artificial intelligence in political campaigns.
The most basic is the right of the author of the AI program to exclude
others from copying, distributing, or otherwise using the program
without his or her consent.  While the scope of this right might be
narrowed somewhat by the fair use doctrine, the first sale doctrine,
and the doctrine of implied license, such narrowing would not be
significant in the context of political campaigns.  Similarly,
parties and campaigns would have a right to protection for the
originality of the AI program.  Again, however, this right is limited
by the fair use doctrine.

2016 was a watershed year for misinformation in politics. In the UK, “fake news” played a big role in the Brexit referendum, and fake news is everywhere. In the future, AI will play a bigger role in election campaigns. We have to be aware of the risks.

I’m personally more concerned about the negative side of AI. I’m not so concerned about how to use it for better campaigns.

Q: What was the main result of the investigation?
A: The PCS panel concluded that the use of AI is compatible with the UK MPs’ code of conduct. In particular, the PCS panel ruled that the use of AI in political lobbying would not amount to a breach of the code of conduct if:
AI is used for the sole purpose of providing constituency services;
AI is used for the sole purpose of making constituency services more efficient;
The use of AI is disclosed to constituents; and
AI does not involve the use of human judgment.
The PCS panel’s conclusions also confirmed that there is nothing in the UK’s Lobbying Act (2014) that prohibits the use of AI in political lobbying.

1. Introduction and Background
Political lobbying is a multifaceted and extensive phenomenon in the United States and in many other countries around the world. Lobbying in the United States is a form of political activity in which citizens and organizations use a variety of methods to influence public policy, and which is conducted at the national, state, and local levels. In the United States, lobbying is defined as “an attempt to influence legislation or administrative action by direct communication with government officials” (Baker, 1993, p. 3).
As defined by the United States Code, “lobbying” includes the following acts:
In any matter on which Federal agencies are authorized to rule or act, persons shall not act under the color of authority derived from the request or authorization of any officer or employee of the executive branch of the Federal Government or under the color of such officer’s or employee’s administrative responsibility for such matter, with intent to influence, without disclosure of the nature of his or her interest, a decision of such agency with respect to such matter made by such agency or officer or employee thereof, if such decision would have an adverse effect upon such person’s business or financial interests.
The term “lobbying” shall also include the use of any personal influence to influence any official of the executive branch of the Federal Government in a matter pertaining to which such person is required to file a registration statement under the provisions of this title, if such official is so specified in the registration statement.
The term “lobbying” shall also include activities directed toward a covered executive agency or the Congress or any of its committees, subcommittees, or members in furtherance of an effort to influence the passage or defeat of legislation or an appropriation, authorization, regulation, rule, or other determination by the Federal Government.
The term “lobbying” shall also include activities directed toward a covered executive agency or the Congress or any of its committees, subcommittees, or members in furtherance of an effort to influence the issuance of a rule, regulation, or administrative order by the Federal Government, including the issuance of a license, grant, or other benefit by the Federal Government.
The term “lobbying” shall also include activities directed toward a covered executive agency or the Congress or any of its committees, subcommittees, or members in furtherance of an effort to influence the awarding of any contract, grant, loan, or other form of financial assistance by the Federal Government.
The term “lobbying” shall also include activities directed toward a covered executive agency or the Congress or any of its committees, subcommittees, or members in furtherance of an effort to influence the making of any determination by the Federal Government, including any suspension, termination, or imposition of sanctions by the Federal Government with respect to a person, organization, or business entity, including the assessment of fees or penalties against such person, organization, or business entity.
(United States Code, 1994, Title 18, Section 1913(c))

1997, a year in which the first animated GIFs were created, the world saw the release of the first feature film, “Titanic.” In that same year, the Internet—an unregulated system of computers—became publicly accessible. Today, 20 years later, the Internet is a critical part of society. The Internet, with its anonymity and interconnectivity, is what brought us Facebook and Twitter, and the power to share photos, videos, and messages from all over the world with the click of a button. The Internet also gave us access to the dark web and, as a result, anonymity for some of the worst cybercriminals and terrorists. The Internet—and the AI that powers it—is a tool that has the potential to drastically improve our society. But, because of its anonymity and the ability to mask identity, it has also created opportunities for people to lie, cheat, and harm others, and has become a tool of the dark web.
“The Internet—and the AI that powers it—is a tool that has the potential to drastically improve our society. But, because of its anonymity and the ability to mask identity, it has also created opportunities for people to lie, cheat, and harm others, and has become a tool of the dark web.”
Ethical and legal concerns, then, have arisen from the power of the Internet to be used for good and evil. These ethical concerns are not new. Internet ethics, in fact, can be traced back to the 1990s. In 1996, the FBI cybercrime unit was formed. In 1997, 150 U.S. businesses were attacked by the “InterNIC Worm.” In 1998, the FBI, Department of Justice, and other law enforcement agencies worked together to bring down the “Bug Trap” criminal hacking group. These events were precursors to the internet’s evolution into the behemoth it is today.
This evolution has not gone unnoticed. In 2012, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) created the National Center for Cybersecurity and Communications. When publishing the results of research using AI, it is recommended that the code used for conducting the analysis be made available in a publicly accessible repository for the purposes of reproducibility and evaluation of results.
1.2 Researchers are encouraged to consult the General Principles for Responsible Use of Data from Research using Artificial Intelligence, which was drafted by the European Commission in consultation with the European Data Protection Supervisor. It presents a set of principles that should be respected in the design and use of AI technologies. These principles are: respect for human rights; transparency; accountability and traceability; ethics; fairness; safety and security; data minimization; and responsible governance.
1.3 Principles 1.4 and 1.5 of the General Principles apply to the use of AI technologies in the context of research with human participants and require that users ensure the following: that research is conducted in accordance with the Regulations of the European Parliament and of the Council on medical devices and in vitro diagnostic medical devices, on the clinical evaluation of medical devices, on medical devices and on the amendment to Directive 2001/83/EC; and that research is conducted in accordance with the European Union Clinical Trials Regulation and the EudraLex Clinical Trials Volume 4A (CTS).
