50% of the answer can be found in the NICTA-led group on accountable systems. It is led by Professor David Abramson, who specializes in AI and accountability, and is part of the new Australian Labor Party’s policy for AI. The other 50% is in the form of a project between NICTA, the University of New South Wales, and the Australian National University. They are working on a system called AutoPolitics that will analyze political speeches and press releases to identify the key political agendas, and will also use a “tone meter” to identify the level of trustworthiness.
Q: How does this compare with the current state of the art?
A: Well, I think the current state of the art is pretty good. Most of the research that has been done has focused on just identifying the agenda, and it is not very good at identifying the level of trustworthiness. One of the reasons for this is that the whole concept of trustworthiness is very subjective. It is very difficult to find an objective way of determining the level of trustworthiness, and the other reason is that tone is notoriously difficult to model using AI.
Q: What are the main challenges?
A: The first challenge is in finding a way to extract agendas in a way that is feasible. This is because of the volume of data that we have. For instance, the Federal Parliament in Australia sits for only 100 days every year, but that means that there are 365 billion words of data in the Hansard. This is a huge amount of data.
Another challenge is that there is no reference corpus that we can use to determine trustworthiness. For instance, when we want to determine if a statement is true, we want to be able to compare it to a reference corpus of true statements. This is not possible because if we have statements that are true, how do we know that they are true? In other words, we have to look at other criteria in order to determine trustworthiness.
Another challenge is that we have to look at the context of the statement. For instance, if we want to determine the trustworthiness of a statement, it is not just a question of looking at the statement in isolation. We have to take into account the context in which the statement was made.
Q: What is your vision for the future of this project?
A: Our vision is to deliver tools that would be able to assist the political community to make better decisions and to communicate better. These tools will be able to assist them to identify what the key political agendas are. For instance, if there is a political party that is saying that it wants to increase taxes on the rich, then it is important to know if that party is actually true to its word. This is because if they do not live up to their word, it is important that the public knows that they are not trustworthy.
Q: What are the other research areas that you are interested in?
A: My main research area is in the field of natural language processing (NLP). I am also interested in data science. For instance, I am interested in machine learning methods for predicting what people are going to say in the future, based on what they have said in the past. This is something that is important for speech transcription, and I think it is also important for the public sector.
The other thing that I am interested in is using AI to detect counter-speech, because we know that if there is a lot of counter-speech, this is a sign that the statement is probably not true. For instance, if there is a lot of counter-speech about vaccines, we can assume that the vaccine is not a good thing.

The data protection audit is one of the most important stages of the compliance process, which allows the company to take a closer look at its data protection activities and assess its compliance with the GDPR.
There are two types of audits:
Internal audit: this type of audit is carried out by the company's Data Protection Officer or by another person authorized by the company. The audit is carried out to check whether the company is complying with the GDPR and the Data Protection Law. The purpose of this audit is to establish whether the company has taken all the measures necessary to comply with the GDPR and to identify any non-conformities.
External audit: This audit is carried out by a third party, which is a data protection officer, data protection authority or other expert. The audit is aimed at checking whether the company complies with the GDPR and the Data Protection Law, but also if the company has adopted the necessary measures to comply with the GDPR and to assess the effectiveness of the measures that it has adopted.
Data Protection Authority's audits
The Data Protection Authority can carry out a data protection audit at any time, in a data controller's premises or in the premises of a processor, as well as by post or by electronic means. The Data Protection Authority can also request information from third parties, such as the processor's employees or suppliers.
The Data Protection Authority will request the company to provide the following information:
Detailed description of the processing activities: the Data Protection Authority wants to know, for each data processing activity, what are the data concerned, who is the data controller, what is the data subject's relationship with the data controller and what is the purpose and legal basis of the processing.
Description of the internal organization and operation: the Data Protection Authority wants to know how the company operates and which measures it has adopted in order to comply with the GDPR.
Description of the technical and organizational measures: the Data Protection Authority wants to know what technical and organizational measures the company has adopted and how the company has ensured that the processing is compliant with the GDPR.

Description of the cooperation of the company with the processor: the Data Protection Authority wants to know which measures the company has taken to ensure that the processor is compliant with the GDPR.
Description of the communication between the controller and the processor: the Data Protection Authority wants to know which communication methods the company has adopted in order to ensure compliance with the GDPR.
List of the data subjects: the Data Protection Authority wants to know which categories of data subjects are involved in the processing of data and what is the legal basis on which the company is relying.
List of the data processors: the Data Protection Authority wants to know the categories of processors, which categories of data they process, where they are located and what is the legal basis on which the company is relying.

When it comes to most information protection laws, organizations are in the dark. For example, a recent healthcare data breach saw 100,000 patient records exposed. The organization said they had the right to be there, but the records were breached and the breach was investigated by the state attorney general’s office.
The records were protected under HIPAA, but the organization didn’t seem to know that.
Many organizations have IT people. Some are really good and know what they’re doing. Others, not so much. Most organizations don’t have anyone specifically responsible for information protection. They know they have to be compliant with laws like HIPAA, but they don’t have a clue how to comply.
Organizations have many tools at their disposal, but when it comes to compliance, they don’t know where to start, much less how to comply. If someone walks in and asks about compliance, the organization may respond with something like, “Let’s see if we’re compliant.” The person then has to go out and start looking for the right documents, which are often buried in someone’s filing cabinet or sitting on some executive’s desk in a drawer.
The average organization has thousands of files on a server and many more in paper files and on desktops. There are no searchable databases with all the information they have, and it’s often in various formats and languages.
As a result, the organization is very likely non-compliant with most laws.
Do you have a list of all your files? Do you know where they are? Do you know what’s in them?
And what about the files you have no idea exist?
The average organization will have to spend hundreds of hours and millions of dollars to clean up the mess if the organization gets caught, and the organization will still be non-compliant. This problem is so widespread that there’s a name for it. It’s called Information Chaos.
One organization’s records are another organization’s problems. When one organization doesn’t know what it has, it’s often a huge problem for another organization, which may be legally required to protect them. When these organizations exchange data, it’s often with the expectation that the other organization will handle it.
Most organizations have a lot of stuff they don’t know they have, and they have to be compliant with laws that require them to protect it. And they don’t know how to do it.
They’re looking for someone to tell them how to do it.

Notify customers of data breaches
Pay fines up to 4 percent of global revenue if the company does not comply with the GDPR

1. Introduction This paper aims to describe the key techniques used by companies to achieve e-commerce security, namely: encrypting sensitive data, disguising data and detecting and evading attack. The concepts of data integrity, authentication, and confidentiality will be discussed. The paper will also discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using certain encryption techniques. 2. Data Integrity “Data Integrity is a measure of the accuracy and completeness of data. Information is complete and accurate when data collected at a system input, and the data are transmitted and stored accurately in the system. It is only when the integrity of data is assured that reliable information can be produced from it. When the integrity of data is compromised, the information becomes useless” (Wang, 2002). The integrity of data is preserved by applying techniques such as hash functions, checksums, and digital signatures to the data. Hash functions such as MD5 and SHA-1 are used to ensure that only the correct data are stored in the database. MD5 is a cryptographic hash function that produces a fixed length string from a variable length input. The hash is used to identify if the data has changed and also to verify the integrity of data transmitted over the Internet. SHA-1 is another cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit hash value from an input of any length. The hash value produced by SHA-1 is smaller than the MD5 hash value and therefore, SHA-1 hash functions are more suitable for use with applications that have limited storage capacity. Hash functions are mainly used to protect the integrity of e-commerce transactions. The hash function takes a given data set and produces a fixed-size hash value that is a representation of the data set (Wang, 2002). The hash value produced can be used to compare with other hash values to verify if the data set has been altered. Digital signatures are used to authenticate data. 1) Honeypots: Companies identify a web page (or page within a website) that is visited by many users who do not fit their marketing demographics. The company then places third-party cookies on these users’ browsers. When these users then visit another website (such as an online news outlet), the third-party cookies are activated and the company collects information about these users.
2) Interest-based marketing: Companies identify users who visit a website that displays interest-based advertisements. These companies then follow these users when they visit other websites in order to collect information about these users.
3) Collaboration: Companies create accounts for their users on third-party websites and then use information they collect from these accounts to target these users with advertisements.
4) Secondary data: Companies use available information (e.g., geographic location) to target advertisements to individuals.

Q: What is a ‘cookie’?
A: A cookie is a small piece of information that a web server sends to a browser, which is then sent back to the server each time the browser requests a page from the server. Cookies allow websites to “remember” information about a user’s preferences, and to enable a site to “personalize” its content for a particular user. Cookies are typically stored in a user’s browser, allowing a website to recognize a user’s computer. Cookies are also used to create ‘web beacons’ that help track a user’s activity on a website.
Q: What is a ‘web beacon’?
A: A web beacon is a transparent graphic image (also known as a pixel tag or clear GIF) on a website or in an email that is used to monitor activity on a website or when a user opens or clicks on an email. Web beacons may also be used to collect information about a user’s computer, such as what type of browser is being used.
Q: What is ‘geolocation’?
A: Geolocation is the process of determining a user’s geographic location. Geolocation may be used by websites to target advertisements to users based on their location.
Q: What is ‘IP address spoofing’?
A: IP address spoofing is a technique used to disguise a user’s IP address (e.g., by “spoofing” it to appear as if it originated from another location). This allows a user’s computer to appear as if it is located in a different place than where it is actually located.

Q: What is ‘Do Not Track’?
A: Do Not Track is a browser-based preference not to be tracked. When users choose to turn on the Do Not Track setting, it sends a signal to websites that a user does not want to be tracked.
Q: What is an ‘ad-blocker’?
A: An ad-blocker is a browser plug-in that prevents ads from being displayed to a user.

A: Do-not-track signals are browser-based preferences that indicate a user’s preference not to be tracked across websites. Do-not-track signals are commonly used by users to prevent companies from collecting information about their activities on websites.

2. The information about an individual that is stored in their own customer data records is often (not always) incomplete. For example, a person may have multiple accounts at different institutions, each of which keeps some of their information. A third party is able to aggregate this data and build a profile that is not available to the individual.
3. In some cases, the collection of data by a third party (usually a data broker) is aided by the collection of personal data by one of the institutions where the individual has an account (this is also referred to as the “pipeline effect”). For example, if a person registers to play a video game and part of the registration process requires them to create an account, the video game company is able to combine the registration details with the individual’s playing history, which may include information on the individual’s location and/or interests, to create a profile.

Aggregation of data is less problematic because individuals cannot usually tell whether the profile is accurate or not.

Individuals may experience a variety of different types of harm as a result of these breaches. These include harm due to identity theft, financial harm, and harm from the violation of individuals' privacy rights.
When an individual's sensitive personal information is exposed, there is a risk of identity theft. For example, a thief could obtain a victim's identity by stealing a purse or wallet, breaking into an individual's home, or even impersonating the victim. The thief could then apply for credit cards, open new bank accounts, or borrow money using the victim's identity. In addition to the victim suffering the loss of money from the theft, the victim may also be held liable for the criminal activities of the thief, such as for a credit card purchase the thief made in the victim's name.

These violations can occur through negligence (for example, leaving a laptop containing sensitive information unsecured) or through intentional acts (for example, sharing a victim's sensitive information with others without the victim's permission). In the latter situation, individuals may suffer harm due to the violation of their privacy when their sensitive personal information is disclosed to others without their consent, or when others act on that sensitive information, such as when a thief obtains a victim's credit card number and uses that credit card to make purchases without the victim's permission.
There are a variety of steps that can be taken to help reduce the harm caused by data breaches. For example, individuals can be proactive in protecting their information. Behavioural tracking is used to make better use of marketing space, so that you don't have to worry about losing money on an advertisement that no one will see.
One method of behavioural tracking is by using cookies, which is done by online platforms like Google, Facebook, Amazon, etc. Cookies are pieces of software that are downloaded onto your computer when you visit a website. This software then stays on your computer even if you close the website and you can't delete it. They also store information about your browsing behaviour, so they know how you navigate websites.
Some websites use advertising networks, so that they don't need to create their own ads. They use a program called DoubleClick. This program places an ad on a website, which tracks the cookies of the users who visit the site. It then places other ads on sites that are visited by people who are likely to be interested in the original ad.
You can get rid of cookies by using the settings on your browser. This may not get rid of all the tracking though, as many websites use other methods of tracking behaviour.
Facebook tracks behaviour through "likes" and "shares". It can tell a lot about you based on what you "like", because these are interests that you have. They also use tracking pixels. These are invisible images that are placed on the website. When you visit the website, the image is downloaded and Facebook knows what you are looking at.
Critics of behavioural tracking say that it is not good for privacy, because the website knows a lot about you. They also say that online platforms need to be careful that they don't overstep the bounds of consumer privacy.
An example of behavioural tracking is when a website, like Facebook or Google, tracks you when you are looking at another website. For example, if you are looking at a website about football, Google or Facebook can see that, and they know your interests. They can then show you football-related ads on other websites.
The opposite of behavioural tracking is called "contextual advertising". This is when you see advertisements on a website that are related to the website that you are looking at. For example, you are looking at a website about cheese, and an ad for a cheese-making company pops up.

Hackers are using the IoT to gain access to individual's devices and gather information, such as their name, passwords, credit card numbers, etc. to be used for fraudulent activity.

Insecure connections: Devices can be set up to use insecure connections that allow hackers to intercept data.

Lack of patches: Many companies don't update their software or patch their devices as frequently as they should, which can also leave the devices vulnerable to hacking.

Set your device to only allow trusted Wi-Fi networks.
Use antivirus software on all devices, and install updates when they become available.
Be careful what information you share on social media.
Be careful what you purchase online.
Change the default password on any IoT devices you have.

In September 2017, the FCC proposed a $25,000 fine against Asurion, a mobile device insurance company, for surreptitiously collecting information about the software, services, and apps installed on users' phones through a fingerprinting script. See FTC Complaint, FCC Order and Consent Decree. The FCC's Order and Consent Decree, which included a consent agreement in which Asurion agreed to delete the fingerprinting script from all servers and cease collecting the data gathered from the script, was later overturned by a District Court Judge who held that the FCC lacked authority to impose civil penalties on an entity that is not subject to FCC regulation and that a $25,000 fine is "grossly inadequate." However, the FCC has appealed the decision, and the FCC's Order and Consent Decree remain in force while the appeal is pending.
2. In September 2019, the FTC settled with a data broker that collected and disclosed consumers' personal information by exploiting a fingerprinting vulnerability in the Android operating system. The FTC complaint alleged that the data broker obtained highly sensitive information, such as a user's Android ID, phone serial number, and phone's locale, when the user merely visited certain websites. The data broker, which did not have a privacy policy or otherwise disclose its data collection practices, then sold the collected data for over 50 cents per piece of data to its clients, including direct marketers, healthcare providers, and media companies. In its settlement order, the FTC banned the data broker from future data collection practices that violate the FTC Act or the GLBA, and required that the data broker delete all of the data collected through the fingerprinting technique, which it did. The FTC also required the data broker to institute a comprehensive privacy program that includes risk assessments, employee training, and independent privacy assessments for the next twenty years.

In the settlement order, the FTC banned the data broker from using the beacon technique, and required it to delete all web browsing data it collected through the technique, which it did.

1. Data Mining and Metadata Analysis
The technology and techniques of data mining and metadata analysis can reveal a great deal about the activities and relationships of individuals, but only if the data is accurate and the metadata analysis tools are sophisticated. The accuracy of the data is important, of course, but even if the data is accurate, a metadata analysis tool could be limited in its ability to analyze the data. For example, the data might be structured, meaning that the data elements have been put into fields, such as first name, last name, and date of birth. In this case, metadata analysis tools that use relational databases would be more powerful.
Metadata analysis tools that do not use relational databases would have to process the data one by one, much as if the metadata analysis was being performed manually. These tools are not so powerful. For example, they may not be able to recognize the difference between a name that is first name and last name and a name that is first name only or last name only. The more structured the data is, the more likely that the metadata analysis tool can be very powerful.
Metadata analysis tools are also often limited by the number of columns in the data. For example, if the data set only has three columns, say, first name, last name, and date of birth, a metadata analysis tool will be limited in its ability to analyze the data. This is because there are only three columns of data to work with. However, if the data set has more columns, say, first name, last name, date of birth, gender, and hometown, then the metadata analysis tool will be able to do more work. It will be able to find the relationships among the various columns of data, such as the relationship between gender and hometown.
Many metadata analysis tools use a number of different techniques to analyze the data. One of the most common tools is relational database theory. Relational databases organize the data so that the elements in each column of the table can be related to the elements in other columns of the table. For example, the metadata analysis tool may look for a common last name in the table. If there are last names, such as Smith, Jones, and Brown, that are common to more than one person, then the metadata analysis tool will find that these last names are related. Similarly, the metadata analysis tool can look for common first names, such as John and Joseph. It can look for common dates of birth, such as September 1, 1956. It can look for common places of birth, such as Los Angeles, California.

This is metadata. Metadata does not contain information about what the data is about. It only contains information about the data. The information about the data can then be used to infer the information about the data. The metadata analysis tool could also use this information to infer the information about the data. For example, the metadata analysis tool may infer that these three patients are the same person by looking for common data. 10. Change your email and social media handles frequently. Use a private email address and create a new social media profile every month. This will help you to have a good privacy protection.

It's not often that you see it in public because it's mostly done in back rooms, and it's done by people who have enough money to buy their way into the data. And it's done mostly in the United States, in California and Illinois and Maryland. But it's done in other countries as well.
A: ​I have had my genomic data stolen multiple times, and I have been part of projects that have had their data stolen. The way it works is that it's pretty simple. You just have to have access to the computing power and the data, and you just look it up. And you have to have some information. So you have to have the data, and you have to have an idea of what you're looking for.
A: ​I think that there are two different problems. I think the first problem is, why do people feel that they have the right to exploit somebody else's genomic data without permission? The second problem, though, is that, how do we prevent people from doing that? I think that it's not a simple problem. I think that the thing that we can do most is educate people on the issues. I think that, if you're given your genomic data, it's your data. I don't think that it should be the government that says, "You have to give it away." I think that it should be up to the individual. I think that if people are given their genomic data, they should have the right to keep it, just as they would have the right to keep their blood, or anything else that they have in their body.
Q: Are there any limitations to the nature of this data?
A: ​There are some problems with the nature of the data. One of the problems is that it's very low-resolution. And one of the things that I'm trying to figure out now is how to do a study that uses the sequenced genome of an individual, but which also measures all of the proteins in the person's body, all of the proteins in the person's blood, and then also measure the metabolites. And this is a big project. We call it the Human BioMolecular Atlas Project, but there's a lot of parts to it. But the reason that I'm doing it is because it's the only way that I know how to study the relationship between genetics and disease. It's the only way that I can study what's going on at the cellular level. And so I think that it's important that we try to be able to study diseases at this level.
Q: What kinds of ethical concerns do you think scientists should be aware of when dealing with this data?
A: ​I think that, ethically speaking, we need to use this information in a way that doesn't cause harm to people. I don't think that it's ethical to do research on people without their informed consent. I think that, one of the problems is that we have a lot of people who are not knowledgeable about genetics and genomics. It's like they're not even aware that there's a possibility that their genomic data can be taken, or that they can be used without their permission. I think that we have to educate people. I think that people who are doing studies need to have a very tight protocol in which they're studying a particular disease. And then, once that's done, they need to publish the results of the study, and they need to have this kind of openness. I think that, if you don't, then it's very easy for people to take this information, and use it for whatever they want. I think that, another thing is that, if you do a study that is based on someone's genomic data and the results are negative, then it's not really right to use it for anything else. I think that, for instance, if you have a study about someone's genomic data, and if the study is negative, then you should not be able to use it for anything else. Because, if you do, then people could say, "Well, I'm going to take my genomic data, and I'm going to do a study on my genomic data, and it's going to come out negative. So I'm going to use it for something else, maybe for drug development." And that's not ethical.

Systems and algorithms are usually biased by the data they are trained on, and that biased data comes from the real world, which is inherently biased. (1) The potential of a system to be biased in the first place, which stems from the type of data it is trained on. If it is trained on a specific population, it may perpetuate the biases that population already has. If the system is not trained on a specific population, it is vulnerable to new forms of bias.
(2) The potential for a system to do harm, which is not limited to cases of automated decision-making. Systems can be abused, the algorithm may not be understood, or it may produce unintended consequences.
(3) The potential for a system to be unduly influenced, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If an automated decision-making system is not being considered on a case-by-case basis, then it is more likely to be biased.
(4) The potential for a system to be manipulated by a party that is not the end-user. This is a major ethical consideration in cases where a system is being used to make a decision that can affect the livelihood of an individual. An algorithmic system can be manipulated by an individual or an entity if it is not accountable to the end-user.
(5) The potential for a system to be inconsistent in its decisions. The decision to place an algorithmic system in a position of power is not always the most ethical decision. In some cases, it may be ethically preferable to make a decision by hand, since automated decision-making can be more biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent than human decision-making.
(6) The potential for a system to be dehumanized, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If the system is treated as a "black box" without an end-user, it will be more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.
(7) The potential for a system to be unethical in its decision-making, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If a system has a way of making an unethical decision without accountability, then it is more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.
(8) The potential for a system to be dangerous, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If the system can make decisions that could potentially harm an individual, it is more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.
(9) The potential for a system to be unfair, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If the system does not follow some form of ethical decision-making, it is more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.
(10) The potential for a system to be unaccountable, which is not a risk to human-based decision-making systems but is a risk to automated decision-making systems. If the system is not accountable to the end-user, then it is more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.
(11) The potential for a system to make decisions that go against the end-user's best interests. An automated decision-making system should do what is best for the end-user. If it is not, it is more likely to be biased, vulnerable to abuse, and less consistent in its decisions.

​Privacy rights are critical for free societies to function properly. The ability of people to live their lives without being monitored by others is one of the cornerstones of a healthy society. Privacy encompasses an individual’s right to control personal data and disclose it selectively. Many people have only recently become aware of the power of data companies have over them and their ability to use this data to make decisions about people’s lives without their consent. The latest advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence take this power to another level. Not only do they allow companies to process vast amounts of data without people’s knowledge, but they also allow companies to gain insights from the data that are often so specific as to be impossible without the data. Even if people were aware of their data being processed, most would not be able to discern how much of this is happening and to what degree their data is being processed in a specific context. These latest technologies make it even more important that people understand what data is being collected about them and how that data is being used.
Q: How do advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence enable data-driven profiling of individuals without their consent and impact fairness in the judicial system?
A: ​Data-driven profiling is an important tool to analyze the behavior of large groups of people to identify the characteristics that make the group successful or that make it vulnerable. These characteristics can then be used to predict the behavior of future groups. This is helpful in identifying groups that may need government assistance and in identifying characteristics that may make groups more vulnerable to social ills such as crime and disease. Properly utilized, these techniques can help society better understand the dynamics of large groups of people. However, when used improperly, it can lead to unfair profiling of groups that are already disadvantaged in society. In order for data-driven profiling to be used properly, it must be carefully controlled by companies and government agencies. Companies must be responsible about the use of their data and must not discriminate against groups of people based on the data they collect. In addition, data-driven profiling should be used to help society as a whole rather than to help companies or government agencies in their own right.

For example, an algorithm may analyze a photo and decide whether it is hateful or abusive without the company doing so itself. In either case, the impact on freedom of speech must be taken into account when developing these technologies.

Section 107 of the copyright law provides: "The fair use of a copyrighted work, including such use by reproduction in copies or phonorecords or by any other means specified by that section, for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research, is not an infringement of copyright. In determining whether the use made of a work in any particular case is a fair use the factors to be considered shall include — (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and (4) the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work." In other words, the use of copyrighted material, such as a photo, for a commercial purpose is fair use only if the copyright holder gives permission, or the use falls under one of the four factors listed above. A commercial use includes advertising, solicitation, or promotion of any product or service. A fair use of a copyrighted work does not include the use of copyrighted material in a manner that would violate the copyright holder's exclusive rights as set forth in 17 U.S.C. § 106.
For more information, visit the U.S. Copyright Office website at http://www.copyright.gov/fair-use/more-info.html.

1. What is a disclaimer?
Disclaimers are a common feature of many contracts. They are generally used to limit a party's liability for a failure to perform or to limit the extent of the party's liability for breach. Disclaimers are commonly used by suppliers and contractors to limit their liability to the value of the materials or services supplied, or to the reasonable value of the services supplied. A limitation of liability clause may be implied in a contract if the parties have acted in a way that implies that they have intended to limit their liability.
2. What are the legal requirements for a disclaimer?
An effective disclaimer must be clear and unambiguous. It must make it absolutely clear to the recipient of the contract that the party is not undertaking to perform to a certain standard. The recipient of the contract must clearly understand that the disclaimer is being relied upon. If the disclaimer is ambiguous, the recipient will be entitled to claim damages for breach of contract.
3. What are the legal requirements for a disclaimer?
A disclaimer is not a defence to a contract that has been breached, so it will not save a party from liability where there has been a breach of contract. It is possible to disclaim liability for contractual breaches, but there must be a contract that clearly indicates the intention to disclaim liability. If the parties intend for a disclaimer to apply to the contract, then they must also intend that liability for a breach of contract be limited to the value of the materials supplied or the reasonable value of the services supplied.
4. What are the legal requirements for a disclaimer?
A disclaimer may not be used to avoid liability that is owed to a third party, such as a debt owed to a creditor or a claim in negligence. For example, a contract may disclaim liability for negligent advice, but it cannot disclaim liability for damage caused by negligent advice.
5. Can a disclaimer be used to disclaim liability for breach of statutory obligations?
Disclaimers cannot be used to exempt a party from their obligations under statute. For example, an employer cannot disclaim liability for failure to provide a safe workplace in circumstances where a statute requires them to provide a safe workplace.

For example, if a party makes a supply of goods or services under a contract, and the goods are defective, the supplier cannot exclude liability for breach of the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993. A supplier may disclaim liability for negligent advice, but they cannot disclaim liability for negligent supply of goods or services.

2018 was a tumultuous year for the online privacy rights of the average internet user. A year ago, no one would have imagined that you could be fined for watching unlicensed streams, or even worse – get arrested for downloading a movie on Kodi.
With such a poor legal environment, it’s no wonder that people turn to VPNs. It’s a simple method of circumventing geo-restrictions – essentially tricking a website to think you’re somewhere else – and not only can it allow you to unlock the world of geo-locked content, but it can also keep your online activity private.
But the legality of using a VPN isn’t as clear-cut as you may think. There are a number of reasons for this and, ultimately, it’s up to you as to whether you’re breaking the law or not.
Firstly, we need to look at the legality of using a VPN to watch geo-blocked content.
In countries like China, VPNs are heavily restricted, with most of the major players being blocked outright. There are also restrictions on the number of connections you can have active at one time and the amount of bandwidth you can use.
This is the case in Russia and in other countries in the Middle East such as Saudi Arabia and UAE. And in the U.S., where streaming services such as Netflix and Hulu are geo-restricted to specific areas, using a VPN to get around these restrictions is still illegal.
But not all countries have such restrictions. In Canada, for example, the VPN laws are considerably more relaxed and it’s not uncommon to find that the popular services like Netflix work perfectly fine with a VPN.
The Canadian VPN laws are so relaxed in fact that it’s possible to watch the entire season 3 of The Americans on the Canadian Netflix before it’s released in the US.
Because of this, it’s not uncommon for American VPN users to head north of the border in order to access the full Netflix catalogue.
But the legality of using a VPN isn’t just limited to geo-restricted content. There are a number of other reasons why you may want to use a VPN.
Security is the most common. People use VPNs to secure their data from snooping eyes and protect their privacy from hackers and other malicious actors. It’s a well-known fact that public WiFi networks are notoriously insecure and this is the reason why many people prefer to use a VPN even when connecting to their own home network.
What makes this particularly important for internet users in countries such as China is that most of the Internet Service Providers (ISPs) that are available in the country are state-run.
Because the country’s government has such a tight grip on the internet, it’s possible for ISPs to snoop on your activity and even monitor and restrict your online activity.
A VPN can be used to keep your connection secure and encrypted. That means that even if your ISP tries to see what you’re up to, it won’t be able to understand what you’re sending and receiving.
So for Chinese citizens, VPNs can protect you against state-sponsored surveillance.
However, the legality of using a VPN for this purpose is a little more grey.
The Chinese government is very strict with their VPN laws and for many years, the country has tried to enforce a ban on VPNs.
And because of the country’s tight grip on the internet, it’s not uncommon for ISPs to throttle VPN users to a point where they can’t even use them.
This is where it gets a little more complicated.
You see, there are two sides to the story.
On the one hand, it’s true that the Chinese government is very strict with the VPN laws and, for the most part, it’s possible to get a VPN that works in the country.
However, this is the case only for VPNs that are registered and licensed in China.
On the other hand, if you want to bypass the VPN ban altogether, you can easily do that by using a VPN that is not registered in China.
For example, a lot of VPNs are registered in Panama, which means that they can effectively bypass the Chinese VPN ban.
This is because the country has no laws against VPNs.

However, they do not provide a clear answer to the question. 17 U.S.C. 106(2) provides that: “Copyright in a work subsists from its creation in a fixed medium of expression and, except as provided in section 105, endures for a limited time.” 17 U.S.C. 102(d) provides that: “A derivative work is a work based upon one or more preexisting works, such as a translation, musical arrangement, dramatization, fictionalization, motion picture version, sound recording, art reproduction, abridgment, condensation, or any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted. A work consisting of editorial revisions, annotations, elaborations, or other modifications which, as a whole, represent an original work of authorship, is a ‘derivative work.’”
The 1994 amendments to the Copyright Act changed the definition of “derivative work” in 17 U.S.C. 102(a)(5), so that a “derivative work” is an “original work of authorship that is based upon one or more preexisting works, such as a translation, musical arrangement, dramatization, fictionalization, motion picture version, sound recording, art reproduction, abridgment, condensation, or any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted.” The 1994 amendments also added 17 U.S.C. 102(b), a definition of “translation,” so that “translation” is “a rendering into another language of a work protected under this title, and a work thus rendered, if it is a work of poetry, a dramatic or musical composition, an engraving, print, or sculpture, is itself a ‘work of authorship’ ….”

25 years in the business of defending employers and educating them on employment law issues has taught me that employers are often surprised at the thought of being called to testify in a lawsuit. Unfortunately, most employers don’t have a plan for this possibility and don’t know what to do when they get a subpoena.
First, you should consult with counsel before responding to the subpoena. In fact, if you receive a subpoena and it’s from a law firm you don’t know, don’t respond at all. It’s not uncommon for unscrupulous attorneys to send subpoenas to employers hoping to intimidate them into paying the subpoenaed documents and attendance fees.
While it’s extremely important that you do not respond to such a subpoena, it’s also important that you don’t ignore it either. If you don’t respond, the attorney may file a motion with the court asking for a contempt order against you for failure to comply with a court order. The attorney may also have grounds to seek sanctions against you for spoliation (intentional or negligent destruction, alteration, or withholding of evidence) if the documents or other evidence sought are not preserved and they’re needed by the opposing party in the case.
Now that you have your lawyer’s advice, what do you do?
You should respond to the subpoena in writing within 15 days, and you must respond in writing to the subpoena even if you plan to attend the hearing in person. When you respond to the subpoena, you should state that you object to the subpoena and explain your objection (for example, you may need time to subpoena documents from another person or company, or the documents are protected by attorney-client privilege). If you do attend the hearing, you should bring along all of the documents that you objected to and prepared a privilege log to show which documents are protected by the attorney-client privilege.
If you do not respond to the subpoena, the attorney may file a motion with the court to compel you to respond.

Copyright law gives the owner of a copyright exclusive rights to reproduce the copyrighted work, to prepare derivative works, and to distribute copies of the work. Copyright law does not prohibit the preparation of derivative works, distribution, or public performance of a work, but it does prohibit the reproduction and distribution of a work without permission from the copyright owner.
Fair use is a legally recognized exception to copyright law. It permits the use of copyrighted works for purposes such as commentary, criticism, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research without permission from the copyright owner.
The 5 factors to consider when assessing whether a use is fair:
The purpose and character of the use.
The nature of the copyrighted work.
The amount of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole.
The effect of the use on the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work.
Any precedents for the use.

1. Avoid high-turnover funds. By definition, a high-turnover fund is one in which most of the portfolio turnover is attributable to taxable events. Funds with high turnover rates generally distribute large amounts of capital gains to shareholders, which are then added to their cost basis and subject to future taxation.
2. Keep your investments in low-turnover funds. Low-turnover funds generally make few sales and purchases. For example, funds that invest in real estate or other illiquid assets are likely to have low turnover.
3. Maximize tax losses. When a fund makes a loss, a shareholder is subject to capital gains tax only on the amount of gain over and above the loss. A fund loss can be used to offset capital gains from other investments.
4. Defer short-term gains to next year. Any gains from the sale of stocks held for less than one year are subject to the ordinary income tax rate. Avoid this higher rate by deferring the sale of such stocks to the next year.
5. Harvest losses from short-term gains. When a stock is held for less than one year, but more than 181 days, the taxpayer may choose to recognize short-term capital gains on a portion of the gain. This strategy may be advantageous when stocks are currently in a rising market and the investor is under-weighted in this sector. If the investor sells shares of a stock at a loss, the loss may be used to offset short-term gains.
6. Sell tax-inefficient investments. Investors should seek to sell investments that are most likely to produce capital gains. If a loss occurs, that loss is subject to the 60-day wash-sale rule. Under this rule, any loss from the sale of a security held for more than 30 days is deductible only if a replacement security is purchased within 60 days before or after the sale.
7. Avoid mutual fund capital gains distributions. Mutual fund distributions can result in taxes for the shareholder if the mutual fund has gains on its portfolio of securities. As a general rule, mutual funds report gains to shareholders for each year. If a fund has significant gains, it must distribute those gains to shareholders. A shareholder must report this income.
8. Defer fund gains until funds are redeemed. If a fund is sold before the end of the tax year, any capital gains from the sale are taxable as short-term or long-term gains. A fund with significant capital gains will have to distribute the gains to shareholders. If an investor does not plan to redeem the fund in the current tax year, consider waiting until the next year to sell the fund.
9. Avoid the wash-sale rule. The wash-sale rule is a tax rule that says if you sell a stock at a loss, the loss is not deductible if you buy substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the sale.
10. Capitalize losses on stocks with high cost basis. There is a 30 percent limit on the deductibility of capital losses. For a loss in excess of this limit, the loss can be carried forward to offset future gains. The maximum amount of tax that can be deducted in one year is equal to the capital gains from sales of all the investor’s stocks.

For example, you can contribute to a traditional IRA even if you are self-employed, but you can’t contribute to a Roth IRA if you are self-employed.
If you are unmarried and your income exceeds the Roth IRA limit ($110,000 in 2012), you can contribute to a traditional IRA and deduct the full amount of your contribution on your taxes.
If you are married and your income exceeds the Roth IRA limit ($173,000 in 2012), you can contribute to a traditional IRA and deduct a portion of your contribution.
And finally, there is no age limit for contributions to traditional IRAs.
If you are near retirement and have a large balance in your traditional IRA, you’ll want to consider converting that balance into a Roth IRA to lower your taxes in retirement.
No matter which account you choose, it’s important to set aside money for retirement as soon as possible.
The earlier you start saving, the more your money has time to grow and the less you’ll have to save to reach your retirement goals.

Most of us aren't as consistent as we should be when saving for the future. In fact, we often make the opposite mistake: we're so focused on saving for the future that we let our present and immediate needs suffer.
But when you invest for retirement, a common-sense strategy called dollar-cost averaging can help you overcome the tendency to let your future needs take a backseat to your immediate ones.
Dollar-cost averaging is a systematic approach to investing where you regularly invest a set amount of money at regular intervals over time.
You divide your total investment into equal installments, then invest those installments at regular intervals.
Why dollar-cost averaging works
The goal of dollar-cost averaging is to reduce the risk of market timing—buying high and selling low.
Instead of investing all of your money at one time, you invest a regular amount over a set period of time. That way, even if the stock market goes down, you'll be investing at lower prices.
The same thing happens when the stock market goes up. You'll be able to buy more shares when prices are high, which will help you take advantage of the upward trend.
Dollar-cost averaging in your 401(k)
With your 401(k) plan, dollar-cost averaging is easy to set up and convenient to use. All you need to do is decide how much you want to invest and when.
Many 401(k) plans offer a set-it-and-forget-it dollar-cost averaging feature that takes away some of the hard work.
All you need to do is decide how much you want to invest and how often—weekly, monthly, quarterly or annually—and then choose a dollar amount that you want to invest.
For example, you might choose to invest $200 every month. The investment would be spread evenly among all your investment options. If one fund does particularly well, you'll invest more in it and less in the others.
The strategy is a bit like a savings plan, with the difference being that your money is invested in the stock market.
You can also set up dollar-cost averaging in an IRA or brokerage account.
Find a dollar-cost averaging strategy that works for you
To decide how much to invest and how often, the first thing you need to do is figure out how much money you can set aside each month.
How much money you have to set aside each month will determine how much you invest and how often. For example, if you have $1,000 each month, you might set aside $100 a month for your 401(k) and $900 to invest in a brokerage account.
Next, you need to figure out the amount you want to invest in each option. For example, if you have $1,000 a month to invest and you decide to invest $500 in each of your 401(k) and brokerage accounts, you'll have $250 left to invest somewhere else, like in a savings account or high-yield online savings account.
Once you've decided where you want to invest, you can use a dollar-cost averaging strategy to make sure you have an even amount of money invested in each option.
Set up dollar-cost averaging in your 401(k)
To set up dollar-cost averaging in your 401(k), ask your employer's human resources department for more information.
If your employer offers a plan with a set-it-and-forget-it dollar-cost averaging feature, you can sign up for it. Or, if your employer offers a choice of investments, you can choose to dollar-cost average among the investment options.
Even if you invest in a target-date fund, a dollar-cost averaging strategy can be a smart way to invest. You can set up a dollar-cost averaging strategy by simply choosing to invest a fixed amount at regular intervals instead of investing your entire contribution when you make your contribution.

Most of us are familiar with the traditional retirement strategy. Work hard, save, and at retirement age, take your assets and invest in a retirement income plan. But, what if we flipped that strategy? What if instead of deferring the tax on your assets, you could actually do something that would turn your tax bill into your retirement check?
Tax-advantaged retirement plans, such as 401(k)s and 403(b)s, allow you to contribute to your retirement by deferring the taxes on your contributions. For example, let's assume that you contribute $10,000 to a 401(k) and you are in the 28% tax bracket. If you make the contribution now, you only pay $2,800 in taxes. If you wait until you are 65, when you take the withdrawal, you will only pay $2,400 in taxes. However, if you were to invest your $10,000 in a taxable account, you would pay $2,800 in taxes now and $2,800 in taxes when you take the withdrawal.
Why is this important? The difference between the $2,400 you would pay in taxes today and the $2,800 you would pay when you take the withdrawal is $400. If you contribute to a tax-advantaged retirement account, you save $400 in taxes on your investment. If you invest in a taxable account, you will have to pay $400 in taxes.
This means that if you put $10,000 into a taxable account today, at retirement, it will be worth $7,600. If you put $10,000 into a tax-advantaged account, at retirement, it will be worth $14,400. This means that if you retire at age 65, the $10,000 that you invested today could turn into $24,000.
At the time that you retire, you will have to pay income tax on the money you take out of your tax-advantaged retirement account. However, if you have contributed the maximum amount to your 401(k) or 403(b) for the year, you may be able to take a tax deduction on your federal income taxes for the amount of your contributions. By contributing to a tax-advantaged retirement account, you are not only deferring the taxes on your assets until retirement, you are also deferring your taxes today.

A structured product is a single contract which provides the investor with a combination of different features, typically yielding a return which is dependent on the performance of another asset, such as a stock or a basket of stocks.
If the underlying asset performs positively, the investor will receive a higher return than the guaranteed return of the structured product. If the underlying asset performs negatively, the investor will only receive the guaranteed return of the structured product, rather than the amount expected.
Because of their complexity, structured products are often marketed aggressively to investors. Typically, a single investor may be exposed to a large number of different underlying assets and risks, yet the investor may only receive one payment upon maturity. For this reason, structured products are not suitable for most investors and should be avoided.
2. If you do wish to invest in structured products, you should select one that matches your investment needs and risk profile. A structured product with a low guaranteed return is appropriate for a very conservative investor, while a structured product with a higher guaranteed return is appropriate for more aggressive investors.
For example, an investor who has a 10-year investment horizon may wish to invest in a structured product that has a 10-year maturity. The investor should also determine if the structured product provides some protection from downside risk, such as a minimum return.
The investor may also want to look for a structured product that provides a guaranteed return for a limited time, such as 5-10 years, then a return based on the performance of the underlying asset thereafter.
If an investor does not have a long-term investment horizon, the investor should not invest in a structured product with a 10-year maturity. If the investor has a short-term investment horizon, the investor should not invest in a structured product with a high guaranteed return or a long-term maturity.
The key to investing in a structured product is to ensure you understand the risks and the potential rewards of the structured product. Structured products, with their large number of features and underlying assets, should not be the focus of an investment portfolio.

​Diversification is a key component of a prudent investment strategy. But one must distinguish between “active” and “passive” diversification, and be aware of their differences. Active diversification means investing in different asset classes that are uncorrelated with each other, such as stocks, bonds, and real estate. Passive diversification means investing in different companies or industries within the same asset class, such as investing in different stocks or different agricultural commodities in the stock market.
If you are interested in “passive” diversification, a logical way to do it is to buy commodities like farmland or timberland through commodity mutual funds. This enables you to invest in agricultural commodities without actually buying the land. Furthermore, these mutual funds offer a range of options that will allow you to construct portfolios that are tailored to your investment needs. For instance, you can invest in timberland in the Pacific Northwest, or farmland in the Midwest.
There are advantages and disadvantages to passive diversification through commodity mutual funds. As a general rule, the more diversification within a commodity, the lower the cost. As an example, a timber mutual fund that invests in timberland in the Pacific Northwest will likely have a lower cost than a timber mutual fund that invests in timberland in the Southeast. However, investors should be aware that passive investments in commodities will be more volatile than those in stocks or bonds.
Bearing these points in mind, I believe there is no simple answer to your question. I would, however, point out that the price of farmland has been rising steadily over the last decade, and I think that the rising price of farmland is related to the growing scarcity of arable land in the United States. This is due to two factors: the amount of arable land is declining because of development and population growth, and the amount of arable land is also declining because of soil erosion. In my view, it is an opportunity to buy farmland now before it becomes too expensive.

However, it is important to note that these vehicles are only tax-exempt at the federal level, meaning that they are subject to state and local taxes. 3) Consider alternative investments. Real estate, commodities, and other alternatives may provide additional opportunities to reduce your tax bill. 4) Be mindful of taxable capital gains and losses. If you’re constantly in and out of funds, you’ll pay taxes on your capital gains and losses. If you can, try to minimize your taxable gains and losses by minimizing the frequency of fund turnover. 5) Understand the tax characteristics of your investments. For example, a fund may advertise that it has a low turnover rate, but not mention that it makes short-term trades. Remember, if the investment has a low turnover rate, your taxable gains will be lower, but your losses won’t. 6) Understand the tax characteristics of the underlying investments. Many mutual funds contain a blend of stocks, bonds, and money market securities. The tax characteristics of each of these underlying securities will vary depending on the underlying security. For example, stocks may have a long-term capital gain while bonds may have short-term capital gains and losses. 7) Understand the tax characteristics of the fund itself. Some mutual funds may be structured as a corporation, while others may be structured as a partnership. Funds that are structured as a partnership will have different tax characteristics than funds structured as a corporation. For example, investors in a corporate-structured fund will pay a tax on dividends regardless of whether they re-invest those dividends or take them in cash. Investors in a partnership-structured fund will only pay a tax on dividends if they re-invest them. 8) Consider strategic tax-loss harvesting. If you believe the market is overvalued, it may make sense to sell some of your investments to realize a capital loss. Your capital loss can be used to offset your capital gains and reduce your overall taxes. However, if you have losses, you’ll want to offset them against gains and not against income. 9) Consider tax-efficient strategies for rebalancing your portfolio. When you rebalance your portfolio, you may need to sell investments to bring your asset allocation back to its target. But if you sell securities with a long-term capital gain, you may pay a tax on the proceeds of your sale. If you’re trying to rebalance your portfolio, it may make sense to sell securities with a short-term capital gain. 10) Review your investment objectives. Tax efficiency is only one factor you should consider when deciding what to invest in. Different investment vehicles may have different tax characteristics. For example, some investors may want to reduce their exposure to capital gains taxes, while others may want to avoid state and local taxes. If you’re investing for income, it may make sense to choose a mutual fund that will pay a dividend or interest. If you’re investing for growth, a fund with high turnover may be the right choice. If you’re a high-net-worth investor, you may want to choose an alternative investment that offers multiple tax benefits. If you’re a retiree, you may want to choose a tax-exempt bond fund. It’s important to consider your tax situation when choosing investments, but it shouldn’t be your only consideration.

Options strategies can be complicated and risky. Before you consider using an options strategy to hedge an equity investment, carefully consider your investment objectives, your risk tolerance, and your need for liquidity. Dr. Ali G. Gharavi, MD, FACC, FSCAI, Director of Cardiac Catheterization Laboratories and the Cardiac Catheterization Laboratory at Saint Francis Medical Center in Peoria, Illinois, says that the causes of irregular heartbeat can be divided into two categories. One category is called supraventricular arrhythmias, which is an abnormal heartbeat that occurs above the ventricles. This can be caused by the abnormal conduction of electrical impulses. The other category is called ventricular arrhythmias, which is an abnormal heartbeat that occurs in the lower chambers. This can be caused by abnormal heart muscle function.
Dr. Gharavi says that there are three types of supraventricular arrhythmias. The first is called atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. This is an abnormal heartbeat that occurs when the upper chambers of the heart, called the atria, are beating rapidly. This causes the heart to beat too fast and can cause symptoms such as palpitations, a feeling of the heart fluttering or racing, dizziness and fatigue.
The second is called premature atrial contractions. These are extra beats that occur in the atria. They cause the heart to beat faster than normal. They can cause symptoms similar to those of atrial fibrillation.
The third is called atrial ectopic beats. These are extra beats that occur in the atria. They can occur in combination with other arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, or premature atrial contractions.
The fourth and last type of supraventricular arrhythmias is called ventricular tachycardia. This is an abnormal heartbeat that occurs in the lower chambers of the heart, called the ventricles. This causes the heart to beat too fast.
Symptoms of a ventricular arrhythmia can include palpitations, a feeling of the heart fluttering or racing, dizziness and fatigue.
Treatment for these types of arrhythmias depends on the type of arrhythmia and its severity. Treatment can involve medications, which can be given in tablet or injectable form, or it can involve a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator.
Dr. Gharavi says that patients who have been experiencing these symptoms should seek the advice of a cardiologist or their primary care physician.

The sleep apnea screening test only takes about 15 minutes. It’s easy to complete and can help you get the treatment you need.
Here’s how to recognize the symptoms of sleep apnea and see if you should get screened.
Sleep apnea symptoms include snoring, choking, and gasping for breath.
Here are a few of the most common symptoms of sleep apnea:
Gasping or choking during sleep
Waking up with a sore throat or dry mouth
Feeling sleepy during the day
Drowsy driving or falling asleep behind the wheel

But how can you get a good night’s rest if your sleep is interrupted by sleep apnea?
Sleep apnea is a condition in which your breathing is interrupted during sleep. This can happen many times during the night.
As a result, you can have a hard time getting a restful night’s sleep. It can also make you tired during the day, which can affect your job performance, school grades, or even your safety on the road.
That’s why it’s important to get help for sleep apnea. If you have sleep apnea, you’re not alone.
In fact, 22 million Americans suffer from sleep apnea. That’s about 8% of all American adults.
Sleep apnea is more common in middle-aged men. But it can affect anyone, even children and teens.
You don’t have to suffer from sleep apnea. You can get relief and sleep better by treating it.
The good news is that sleep apnea is often treated effectively with a simple device called a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine.
Your doctor can prescribe a CPAP machine. This machine provides a steady stream of air through a mask that you wear while you sleep.
The stream of air keeps your airway open so you can breathe and sleep well. You can feel better the next morning, and the morning after.
What are the sleep apnea symptoms?
Many people don’t realize that they have sleep apnea. They may just think they’re tired or have trouble sleeping.
But if you experience some of these symptoms, you should get screened for sleep apnea:
Unexplained fatigue and sleepiness
Congested or runny nose in the morning
Falling asleep while working, reading, or watching TV
Breathing through your mouth while sleeping
If you have any of these symptoms, you should get screened for sleep apnea. This is a simple, non-invasive, at-home test.
Your doctor can do a sleep apnea screening test. The test takes only 15 minutes. It’s quick and painless.
A sleep apnea screening test uses a small sensor called an actigraph. The sensor attaches to your wrist like a watch. You can wear it all night while you sleep.
The sensor can tell how many times you stop breathing and how many times you wake up while you’re sleeping.
The information is sent to a computer. A trained sleep specialist will look at your results.
Based on your results, your doctor can determine if you have sleep apnea. You may be referred to a sleep specialist for a polysomnogram (PSG).
A PSG records your heart rate, breathing, brain waves, muscle movements, and oxygen levels while you sleep.

If you have sleep apnea, you should talk to your doctor. They can help you get the right treatment.
They can help you get a sleep apnea machine or device. This is the best way to get relief from your sleep apnea symptoms.
If you have central sleep apnea, a CPAP machine may not be the right treatment for you. Your doctor will help you decide what’s best for you.

Your doctor may prescribe a preventive medication, which you take every day to prevent migraines before they occur. You may also be prescribed a triptan if you experience migraine symptoms. For example, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), a type of psychotherapy that teaches you ways of thinking and behaving more adaptively, is an important tool in the treatment of bipolar disorder. You and your psychiatrist may collaborate to develop a treatment plan that may include medication, CBT, and other strategies, such as lifestyle changes. Research studies have shown that people with bipolar disorder who adhere to their treatment plan benefit most. This means that you may take your medication every day and participate in your psychotherapy regularly, as prescribed.
Q: How can I get my family member to comply with his or her treatment plan?
A: ​​​​Families can play a critical role in helping a family member with bipolar disorder adhere to his or her treatment plan. To be helpful, they need to understand the disorder, have realistic expectations, and know how to set limits. They should be supportive without enabling. They can do this by being respectful, non-judgmental, and compassionate. Most importantly, they can have open, honest discussions with their loved one about his or her treatment plan. This will help the family member feel more motivated to stick with the treatment plan. The most important treatment goal is to prevent relapses. This means that the family member must take his or her medication, keep his or her regular therapy appointments, and participate in other healthy lifestyle behaviors, such as getting enough sleep and avoiding alcohol and recreational drugs.
Q: My bipolar symptoms started when I was 13 years old, and I have been hospitalized four times since then. My psychiatrist has tried several medications, but none have helped me. What should I do now?
A: ​​​​Medication trials are an important part of the treatment process. Unfortunately, many patients with bipolar disorder are not helped by the first medication they try. In fact, about 25 percent of patients with bipolar disorder do not respond to their first medication. Therefore, it is important to work with your doctor to find the right combination of medications. Sometimes it takes several medication trials to find the right medication. Once you find the right medication, the goal is to stay on it for six months to a year and see if your moods and functioning improve. If you have relapses, you may be hospitalized while your doctor tries different combinations of medications. If you have not had any good results with medication, it is important to talk with your doctor about possible psychotherapy options, such as CBT, or other treatments, such as lithium or ECT.
Q: I have been hospitalized several times for my bipolar disorder, and I am concerned about side effects of medications. How can I reduce my risk of side effects?
A: ​​​​There are many medications used to treat bipolar disorder. Fortunately, most are well-tolerated. However, some people may have side effects that require them to change medications. Sometimes, doctors may even switch back and forth between medications to find the best combination for each patient. Other people may require additional medications to help prevent side effects. For example, people taking lithium should take a low dose of a thyroid hormone pill to help prevent a low thyroid. People taking olanzapine (Zyprexa) may be given a high dose of a thyroid hormone pill and a low dose of clozapine (Clozaril) to help prevent low blood sugar. People taking risperidone (Risperdal) may require a low dose of lithium to prevent a low thyroid. Side effects can also be managed by titrating the medication, or starting the medication at a low dose and gradually increasing the dose to the therapeutic level.

3.5 million Americans over the age of 40 are afflicted with macular degeneration, an eye disorder that causes visual impairment and loss of central vision. The Center for Disease Control lists age-related macular degeneration as the leading cause of blindness in the United States.
The most common types of macular degeneration are dry macular degeneration (also known as atrophic or non-neovascular) and wet macular degeneration (also known as neovascular or exudative).
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a chronic disease that occurs as a result of damage to the retina of the eye. The retina is the back of the eye where light rays are focused. The macula, located in the center of the retina, is the part of the retina that is responsible for central vision, the sharp, straight-ahead vision that is used for seeing objects clearly and for common daily tasks such as reading and driving.
In the early stages of AMD, there are usually no symptoms. There are two forms of AMD: dry and wet. In the dry form, the vision loss is gradual. In the wet form, vision loss occurs rapidly.
Age-related macular degeneration is the most common cause of legal blindness in people over the age of 65 in the United States. It usually occurs in both eyes.
If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, you should consult your eye care professional as soon as possible.
There is no cure for age-related macular degeneration, but there are treatments that can slow down or stabilize the disease and improve vision.
These treatments include laser treatments, injections, and a new drug treatment called Lucentis, which has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for use in treating wet macular degeneration.
Another new drug called Eylea has been approved by the FDA for use in treating wet macular degeneration. These drugs are injected directly into the eye and can help slow or stabilize the disease.
These treatments can improve vision in most people. In some cases, vision may not improve, but will stabilize. These treatments do not cure the disease. They only help improve vision and they do not work for all patients.
Early diagnosis is crucial, so if you are experiencing any symptoms, make an appointment with your eye doctor. Early diagnosis can help delay the progression of the disease and its potential to cause vision loss.
Other possible treatments may be suggested by your eye care professional, based on the type of AMD you have.
There are a number of foods that can help prevent age-related macular degeneration.
The most important is to eat a diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which include the fish oils. The best sources of omega-3 fatty acids are fish such as salmon, mackerel, tuna, herring, and sardines.
Other good sources of omega-3 fatty acids are walnuts, flax seed, soy, and tofu.
Blueberries, blackberries, and strawberries are also good foods to eat.
You should eat plenty of leafy green vegetables, as well as foods that are high in vitamin C.
You should also get plenty of exercise.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is characterized by abdominal pain or discomfort and changes in bowel habits. About 20% of people are affected with this condition.
IBS can affect people at any age from children to adults. In some cases, it may last for a long time and can be incapacitating. The exact cause of IBS is unknown. However, it is likely due to a combination of factors. These factors may include:
Psychological stress or anxiety
Genetics (family history of IBS)
Nutritional deficiency (vitamin B12 or iron)
Certain medications, such as antibiotics, painkillers or laxatives
IBS is a chronic condition, which is means it lasts a long time. Its symptoms tend to come and go. The symptoms may include:
Bloating, swelling and excess gas
Changes in bowel habits such as constipation, diarrhea or alternating both
Having pain that is relieved after a bowel movement
Feeling bloated, gassy, or crampy
The main goals of treatment are to improve bowel function and reduce symptoms. Making changes in your daily routine can also help prevent or reduce symptoms.
There is no single treatment that works for everyone. Treatment will depend on the individual. A team of health care professionals may help manage IBS.
Depending on your symptoms, the treatment approach will include one or more of the following:
There are many medications used to treat IBS.
Anti-diarrheal medications
For diarrhea, these medications may slow the passage of food and fluid through the bowel.
Anti-constipation medications
For constipation, these medications may stimulate contractions of the intestinal muscles and promote bowel movements.
Anti-spasmodic medications
For pain and cramping, these medications may help relax the intestinal muscles.
Laxatives can help improve bowel movements.

Many of these are available without a prescription. They include:
Products containing psyllium, such as Metamucil or Konsyl
Slippery Elm and Marshmallow
Saccharomyces boulardii and Lactobacillus GG
Fiber supplements can help relieve diarrhea.

Foods high in fiber include:
