Q: Is sclerotherapy a painful procedure?
A: The procedure can be uncomfortable for a short time.
A: You may be instructed to walk for a short time after the procedure.
Q: How long do the veins disappear after sclerotherapy?

A: It depends on the number of veins that are being treated.

2004 is a very busy year for elective surgery. This is due to a combination of factors including an aging population, the high costs of health care and the rapid growth in technology. While the possibility of complications exists with every surgical procedure, elective surgery is usually the safest time for patients to have surgery. However, the possibility of complications is not zero.
Patients should be aware that the chance of complications varies for different types of surgery. For example, the chances of complications associated with gallbladder surgery are lower than those associated with hip replacement surgery. For more information on this topic, please go to:
http://www.facs.org/public_info/patient/surveillance/survey/surveystats04.html
This is a good place to start and ask questions about specific surgical procedures.
Q: What are the risks of having surgery at this time?
A: The surgical community is fully aware of the impact of the shortage of nurses, pharmacists and anesthesiologists on the daily operation of the health care system. Your doctor may have to cancel a surgery, delay your surgery or reschedule your surgery. The length of your surgery may be extended because of the shortage of operating room time.
The risk of surgical complications depends on the type of surgery you are having, but the shortage of health care professionals does not increase the risk of complications for elective surgery.
You should ask your doctor about the risks of your individual surgical procedure.
Q: What can patients do to help?
A: Patients should be aware that the doctor is not the only person working on their surgery. An entire team of health care professionals are involved in the care of each patient. If a surgery is cancelled, delayed or rescheduled, it is important that the patient call to reschedule their surgery as soon as possible. This will make it possible for the entire team to prepare for the new surgery date.
Patients should continue to take their medications as prescribed. This will help to minimize the risk of developing any potential health problems that could lead to surgery. Patients should try to eat a healthy diet and exercise regularly. This will help them to get into the best health possible before surgery.
Patients should keep in contact with their doctor to make sure that all tests have been done and all questions have been answered. Patients should make sure that they understand what to expect before, during and after their surgery.
Patients should be aware that there are many choices available to them in the health care system. Patients should ask questions about their health care and if they are not satisfied with the answer, they should seek out another source of information.
Q: Can the surgeon reduce the possibility of a complication?
A: The surgeon can help by planning surgery as well as possible. There are many factors that the surgeon cannot control, however, including the hospital's ability to staff the operating room and the anesthesiologist's ability to staff the recovery room. Your doctor is working with everyone in the health care system to reduce the potential for a complication to occur.
Q: Will my health insurance cover the cost of my surgery?
A: This is a complex question. There are several factors that determine whether or not your insurance will cover the cost of your surgery.
If you have been advised by your doctor that you need surgery, then you should call your insurance company to find out what types of questions your insurance company will ask before approving your surgery. This will help you to make an informed decision on the best day to have your surgery.
If you are having a problem with your insurance company, you should contact your state insurance regulator or the Office of Health Insurance Programs at 1-800-842-0004. The Office of Health Insurance Programs will help you to contact the correct insurance regulator.
You can find out more about your insurance coverage by contacting the Office of Health Insurance Programs at 1-800-842-0004.

A: Yes. Overweight people are more likely to suffer from hypertension than thin people.
Q: What is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure?
A: The systolic pressure is the top number in the blood pressure reading. It is the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats. The diastolic pressure is the bottom number and is the pressure in the arteries when your heart is at rest.
Q: Can my blood pressure rise when I’m nervous or angry?
A: Yes, but your blood pressure usually returns to normal when you calm down.
Q: Can I reduce my blood pressure through lifestyle changes?
A: Yes. Regular physical activity (45 min/day), a healthy diet, no smoking, and reduced alcohol consumption can lower your blood pressure.
Q: Why do my blood pressure numbers change when I measure them?
A: Blood pressure varies from day to day. It also varies from one minute to another. The numbers on your blood pressure monitor are the average of several readings taken in a minute.

A: Yes, it is safe to take insulin if you smoke. Smoking may make it harder for your body to use insulin. Taking insulin may make it easier for your body to use insulin and help you have good blood sugar control.

10 to 20 percent of people who have OCD respond well to exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy, but the rest are not helped by it. The best option for them is a drug such as fluoxetine (Prozac), which has been shown to be particularly effective in OCD. There are also other drugs that are effective in OCD, but fluoxetine is the most well-studied. Some people respond better to a drug like citalopram, which is similar in its action to fluoxetine but is thought to be less likely to cause sexual side effects. There are also newer medications, such as sertraline, escitalopram, and paroxetine (Paxil), which have less of a sexual side effect but may have more of a side effect of insomnia. Often, if there are no side effects, people will take a drug like fluoxetine in doses as low as 10 milligrams. The most common dose is 20 milligrams, although some people may require higher doses of 40 milligrams. But starting with a dose as low as 10 milligrams can be an effective option for some people.
Benzodiazepines such as diazepam (Valium) are not the best option for treating OCD, although they are sometimes prescribed for managing the anxiety that may accompany the disorder. There are more effective medications for treating the anxiety.
Q: Can taking a drug like fluoxetine prevent my obsessive-compulsive disorder from becoming severe?
A: For most people, fluoxetine may prevent obsessive-compulsive disorder from becoming severe. In studies, about one-third of people had a reduction in symptoms, another third were unchanged, and the remaining third had an increase in symptoms.
Q: I've heard that some people have an allergic reaction to SSRI antidepressants. Is there any truth to this?
A: I've heard the same thing. There have been people who have experienced an allergic reaction to SSRI antidepressants. I don't know why this happens, but the best advice is to take the lowest dose possible and to stay on the medication for at least six weeks. If a drug isn't working for you, and your doctor thinks it's a good option, you should try it at a lower dose, because some people have a greater sensitivity to a drug than others. Sometimes a doctor will suggest trying a different antidepressant, rather than going back to the same one with a lower dose.
Q: Is it safe to take SSRI antidepressants while pregnant?
A: Fluoxetine and sertraline are not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy. The current thinking is that it's better to wait a few months before taking these drugs. There are many reasons for this: peripheral neuropathy can be caused by systemic diseases such as diabetes, vascular disorders, infections, toxins, or even trauma. There are also many medications that can cause the same effects, so it’s important to keep a list of any medications you’re taking and discuss them with your doctor.
Most peripheral neuropathies are progressive, meaning they get worse over time. However, if you are diagnosed with peripheral neuropathy, you have the opportunity to get an early diagnosis and treatment, which can slow or even halt the progression of your neuropathy.
Dr. Chris Pine, a neurologist at the Carroll County Medical Center, is a specialist in diagnosing and treating patients with peripheral neuropathy. He works with a team of neurologists at the medical center, including Dr. Andrew Brown and Dr. Michael Chan, to provide comprehensive, expert care.

What are the symptoms of peripheral neuropathy?
The symptoms of peripheral neuropathy can vary depending on the cause and the location of your nerve damage. In addition to numbness and tingling, you might also experience:
pain, burning, or electric shock sensations
sores or ulcers on the toes, feet, or hands
the inability to feel pain, temperature, or touch
The Carroll County Medical Center’s neurologists can help you determine the best treatment for your condition.
What causes peripheral neuropathy?
There are many reasons for peripheral neuropathy, including:
medications, such as chemotherapy or other toxic drugs, antibiotics, or chemotherapy
autoimmune diseases, such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and myasthenia gravis
traumatic injuries such as fractures or burns
toxins, such as lead or mercury
How can I prevent peripheral neuropathy?
While there is no sure way to prevent peripheral neuropathy, there are steps you can take to lower your risk:
Take care of your feet. Use proper footwear, keep your feet clean and dry, and avoid getting your feet wet for too long. If you have diabetes, check your feet every day.
Don’t smoke. Smoking damages your nerve cells, so quitting smoking can help reduce your risk.
Don’t drink a lot of alcohol. Alcohol is toxic to your nerves, so limit your alcohol intake to no more than one drink a day.
Eat a healthy, well-balanced diet. A diet rich in fruits and vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products can help prevent peripheral neuropathy.
Get plenty of exercise. Regular exercise can help prevent peripheral neuropathy.
Seek treatment for diabetes. Diabetes can cause a loss of sensation, which increases your risk of developing neuropathy. It’s important to keep your diabetes under control.

10 years ago, my wife was diagnosed with early stage macular degeneration. We were told she had dry macular degeneration and that it was very unlikely to progress to wet macular degeneration.
A few months later, she had sudden vision changes and was diagnosed with wet macular degeneration.
After her laser treatment, she has had no further vision changes.
She continues to have excellent peripheral vision, and has no problems driving.
Although her vision is still much better than mine, she had to stop working as a nurse.
I don't know what to think, because I'm terrified of having macular degeneration.
My vision is also good, so I'm not worried about losing my vision, but my wife can't work.
I'm afraid I might be heading for the same thing.
I'm very worried that my vision will continue to deteriorate.
Any thoughts or comments would be greatly appreciated.
A: It is important to realize that it is not the "wet" (neovascular) form of macular degeneration that is devastating to vision, but the "dry" form that accounts for 90% of all cases.
The "dry" form is marked by an accumulation of "drusen", which are deposits of sub-cellular material, on the macula.
The "wet" form is marked by the growth of new blood vessels on the surface of the retina.
These new blood vessels can leak, resulting in rapid vision loss.
The most likely cause of the sudden vision changes in your wife was a growth of new blood vessels on the surface of the retina.
The good news is that laser treatment of the retina was successful in preventing the retina from being damaged further.
The bad news is that the "dry" form of macular degeneration is an incurable disease that cannot be treated.
The only thing that can be done is to monitor the disease to see if it progresses.
If the "dry" form of macular degeneration progresses, the only way to slow it down is with daily use of an anti-oxidant vitamin (i.e., vitamin C, vitamin E, beta carotene).
I suggest that you and your wife visit the website of the Macular Degeneration Research Foundation and read the information they have on macular degeneration.
If you have further questions, you can email them to macular@macular.org or call their toll-free number at 1-800-222-3937.
I hope this information has been helpful.

2008 was the first time cosmetic surgery was not associated with death, and that year there were 11.6 million procedures. In 2010, there were 13.7 million procedures. The number of operations has not slowed, and with the exception of a decline in 2009, the statistics show a clear upward trend. According to the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, the number of surgical and minimally invasive cosmetic procedures increased 5 percent from 2010 to 2011.
In a study published by the Archives of Dermatology in 2011, there were 3.5 million cosmetic surgical and minimally invasive procedures performed in 2010. Out of those procedures, complications occurred in 6.2 percent of all procedures. The number of complications was highest in the 18- to 44-year-old age group.
While the odds of complications are relatively low, it is important to understand the potential risks. Although complications are rare, it is still important to be prepared for the rare, but possible, occurrence.
There is a lot of variation in patient risk factors, so it is important to find a surgeon who is certified and experienced in your procedure and who takes time to make sure you understand all the risks.

There should also be a preoperative consultation to discuss your medical history, medications, allergies, and the procedure, as well as the potential risks and benefits.
Although it is impossible to eliminate all risks, you can minimize the potential for complications by choosing a qualified surgeon and having a thorough preoperative evaluation.
Q: What is the likelihood of a complication and what are the most common complications?
A: Although cosmetic surgery has a very low complication rate, there are a few important things you should know. First, you should not allow anyone to pressure you into having a surgical procedure you are not comfortable with. As with any surgical procedure, there is always a risk of complications.
One of the most common complications is swelling. Swelling is normal and goes down slowly, but it can be minimized by applying ice to the face for the first 48 hours after surgery. The swelling may last for one to three weeks, and sometimes takes several months to go down completely. Swelling can be minimized by wearing a headband while sleeping, keeping your head elevated, and taking a pain reliever as recommended by your doctor.
The risk of bleeding increases with age. If you are taking any blood-thinning medications, make sure to inform your surgeon so they can monitor your condition. If you have a history of bleeding problems, or you are taking aspirin, ibuprofen, or any other blood-thinning medication, tell your surgeon.
Post-operative infections are rare, but they can occur in any surgical procedure. To minimize the risk, make sure to keep the wound clean and dry for at least 24 hours. If there is any sign of a skin infection, such as redness, swelling, or drainage, call your surgeon immediately.
Scarring is a frequent complication of surgery. Scars fade over time. In some cases, the scar may be raised and thick. It may also be wide and red initially, but it will fade with time. Certain procedures, such as a rhinoplasty (nose job), may leave some permanent swelling and slight asymmetry.
Q: Are there any other complications of cosmetic surgery I should be aware of?
A: Other rare complications of cosmetic surgery include nerve damage, internal bleeding, blood clots, and poor wound healing. Most cosmetic surgeons have dealt with these complications before and can usually help manage the problem.
The ASPS also recommends that all patients choose a surgeon who is certified and experienced in their procedure and who takes time to make sure you understand all the risks. Ask your surgeon if they have a formal training program or have completed an accredited surgical fellowship.

2) If you are over-eating, your bowels are probably not getting enough fibre. Avoid foods that are high in fat, and high in sugar. Examples of these foods are: pastry, ice-cream, biscuits, cream sauces, cakes and pastries. Eat more fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole-grain breads, seeds and nuts.

4) Avoid drinking too much alcohol. It is very bad for your bowels and it can also make your symptoms worse.
5) Drink plenty of water to keep your bowels working.
6) Avoid drinking carbonated drinks. They can make your bowels move too quickly.
7) Avoid foods that have been processed. Eat more fresh foods.
8) Avoid spicy foods if your symptoms are bad.
9) If you have diarrhoea, avoid foods that contain high levels of fat.
10) Don’t take antibiotics if you have diarrhoea. Antibiotics kill the good bacteria in your bowel and can make your symptoms worse.
11) If you have constipation, eat more foods that contain fibre. These foods are: whole-grain bread, brown rice, nuts, seeds, legumes (beans, chickpeas, lentils), apricots, strawberries and apples.

15) Eat more foods that contain resistant starch (such as potatoes, sweet potatoes, plantains and green bananas).
16) Eat more foods that contain sorbitol (such as pears, apples, apricots, prunes, peaches, plums, cherries, mangoes, nectarines, grapes, kiwi fruit and pineapple).
17) Drink more water. It’s important to drink plenty of water to keep your bowels working.
18) Exercise regularly, but don’t overdo it.
19) Keep active and don’t sit around too much.
20) Don’t take laxatives. They don’t fix the problem.
21) Don’t take pain medications that contain opiates. These medications slow down your bowels and can make your symptoms worse.
22) If you have diarrhoea, try to keep your bowels moving. Go to the toilet as soon as you feel the urge.
23) If you have constipation, try to keep your bowels moving.
24) Don’t strain when you have a bowel movement.
25) Don’t ignore your bowels. If you are worried about going to the toilet, and you don’t go, the muscles in your bowels can get weak, and your bowels will not work properly. This can make your symptoms worse.

2016 has brought the release of some new and exciting medicines and treatment options for patients with rheumatoid arthritis. As we have been following the research and clinical trials for these medicines in the last 24 months, it has been very exciting to see the development of treatments that can work for a much greater proportion of patients.
The newest drug approved for rheumatoid arthritis is called Secukinumab. This medicine works by targeting and interrupting the inflammation process. By blocking the effects of inflammation in the body, the RA symptoms and signs of the disease will be able to be controlled. This is very exciting news for patients as this is the first drug that works in a new way to treat rheumatoid arthritis.
Another very exciting treatment that has been released is called Etanercept. This medicine has been used for many years to treat patients with RA. Etanercept works by interrupting the inflammation process, which helps to reduce the joint damage that can occur in RA. However, Etanercept can only work for up to 6 months and then the patient’s symptoms start to return. This is due to the body developing antibodies that can ‘block’ the effects of Etanercept, therefore it is not able to work in the body anymore.
The newest treatment for Etanercept is called Biosimilar. Biosimilar medicines work in exactly the same way as Etanercept, however there are no differences in how the medicine works and its safety.
Two new medicines called Abatacept and Adalimumab were also approved this year for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Both of these medicines work by interrupting the inflammation process in the body, which helps to reduce the joint damage that can occur in RA.
Finally, the first medicine that targets the disease process in RA, called Rituximab, was approved for the treatment of RA. This medicine works by targeting the immune cells that play a role in the destruction of the joints and other organs in RA. This is a very exciting drug and is used to treat patients who do not have any other treatment options left.
Dr Amy Smith is an Rheumatologist based in Perth, Western Australia. You can find more information about her on her website www.rheumatologywa.com.au. She can be contacted on 0420 556 028 or by email at info@rheumatologywa.com.au.

​Your question shows your passion to address your OCD, which is an admirable trait. I love it when my patients are proactive about their health. You may be at the point where you are looking at every possible treatment option for your OCD.
It's important to start with the basics. If you have obsessive thoughts and a compulsion to repeat actions, your primary care provider will likely recommend a medication called fluoxetine, commonly known as Prozac. There are several more complex drugs that may be prescribed, but Prozac is the simplest medication to try first. You should be working with a doctor who is trained to treat mental health issues. In some cases, medication may not be the best approach, and there are alternative treatments that your doctor can recommend.
If the Prozac is not effective, your doctor may recommend another type of antidepressant, and may also recommend cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to help you understand your compulsions and your obsessions and develop coping skills to better manage your OCD.
Your doctor may also recommend psychotherapy. There are several types of psychotherapy that are helpful in treating OCD.
Because OCD can be a very distressing disorder, it can be difficult to learn to cope with the symptoms. If you are motivated, you may have better success. It's important to find the treatment that works for you and your lifestyle.

Q: My doctor prescribed me a potent antidepressant to treat my pain. Is it dangerous?
A: All potent antidepressants have been shown to be safe and effective for use in the treatment of painful conditions such as fibromyalgia, myofascial pain, headaches, and so on. Although the mechanism of action is not fully understood, there are specific serotonin receptor subtypes that are involved in mediating pain signals. If the pain is very severe, it might be helpful to add an anticonvulsant or a narcotic to the antidepressant, as well as a muscle relaxer.
Q: I have been on an antidepressant for three years. I am worried about being dependent. Should I stop taking it?
A: Although there is no real risk of developing a physical dependence, you may have noticed that your mood and energy levels have changed over the years. If you have had a positive response, you should not stop taking it abruptly, but taper off by reducing the dose gradually. If you are concerned about the long-term effects, you might want to talk to your doctor about whether it is safe for you to stop the medication.
Q: I had a series of miscarriages and now I am taking an antidepressant. Will this cause the next pregnancy to end in miscarriage, too?
A: No. The use of antidepressants during pregnancy does not increase the risk of miscarriage.
Q: I am on an antidepressant, but I am not feeling very good. Should I change my medication?
A: This can be a difficult decision, and it is not a good idea to make a change without talking to your doctor. There are a variety of factors to consider. You should also know that the fact that you are not feeling well does not mean that you are not getting the full benefit from the medication. Sometimes, it takes a while for the antidepressant to work, and you may not notice any improvement for several weeks to several months. If the medicine is not working, you and your doctor should think about other ways to treat your depression, such as increasing the dose of the antidepressant, switching to another antidepressant, adding a second medication, or adding a form of psychotherapy.
Q: I have a family history of depression. Can I avoid developing depression by taking an antidepressant?
A: Unfortunately, we do not have a good way of predicting who will get depression in the future. However, taking a medication can certainly help to reduce your risk of developing depression.
Q: My friend and I are taking antidepressants and we are concerned that we may be addicted to them.
A: A medication is not addictive if you are taking it as directed. There is no evidence that taking an antidepressant for a prolonged time causes physical or mental dependence.

Q: My parents are now in their late 70's and early 80's. I want to be sure that they are protected if they need nursing home care. How can I do that?

These assets and income are referred to as "countable resources." Your parents may be eligible to protect up to $116,000 in countable resources through the use of a Medicaid Qualifying Trust.
Q: What are some strategies to help pay for nursing home costs?

If your parents' assets do not exceed $116,000, it may be possible to transfer assets to their children without affecting Medicaid eligibility. (This is called a Medicaid Gap Trust.) Q: What should I do if I suspect someone is experiencing anaphylaxis? A: 911 Emergency If you or someone you are with has an allergic reaction, the most important thing to remember is to call 911. This can be done from a cell phone, if one is available, or by leaving the phone on the ground and calling. The operator will tell you what to do.
If the reaction is minor, do the following:
Remove the person from the situation that caused the reaction. This can be done by placing the person in a cool place or by removing them from the environment that caused the reaction.
Cool the person down. If the reaction is an allergic reaction, the person may be experiencing anaphylaxis. This is a severe allergic reaction that needs immediate medical attention.
If the person is breathing, make sure the airway is clear by turning the person on their side to open up their airway. Then give two doses of the epinephrine auto-injector. After this, call 911.
If the person is not breathing, start CPR. If the person is in the water, make sure they are floating up and down with their head above the water, then give two doses of the epinephrine auto-injector. After this, call 911.

Governments and international organizations have always been involved in the processing and implementation of international instruments, and this was the case before the 1951 Convention. The more recent international instruments, such as the 1990 UN Convention against Torture, the 1995 UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, and the 2000 UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, have also required governments to collaborate with international organizations and NGOs in their implementation. This is in part due to the fact that international organizations and NGOs have expertise in these areas, and in part due to the fact that these instruments are generally seen as being of universal application and thus need to be implemented in many different countries. In the context of the 1951 Convention, for example, the Convention allows for the involvement of international organizations, NGOs and other non-governmental entities in the implementation of the Convention, including the provision of financial and technical assistance, and the review of resettlement practices. The primary goal of this is to ensure that the Convention is implemented effectively and with respect for human rights. This is evident in the different aspects of the Convention, including: (a) the Refugee Status Determination procedure (see question 2 below); (b) the Asylum Seeker Procedures (see question 2 below); (c) the International Protection (see question 3 below); and (d) the Resettlement (see question 4 below).
In order for international organizations and NGOs to be involved in the implementation of the 1951 Convention, the Convention requires that governments agree to this in a national policy on refugees. This policy, adopted by governments, is the main source of guidance to domestic organizations and agencies in relation to the implementation of the Convention. Q: What are the different models of managing migration through diplomacy?
A: The international community has several instruments that it can use to manage migration flows through diplomacy. These instruments can be categorized into three main models: bilateral agreements; regional or multilateral agreements; and institutional arrangements.
Bilateral agreements are the most common type of international agreement used to manage migration flows. While bilateral agreements are generally not legally binding and are often discretionary, they can facilitate co-operation between states in a number of ways. In particular, they can be used to manage the regular movement of people through the adoption of safe third country principles. Bilateral agreements can also be used to help improve conditions in the country of origin by reducing the need for people to migrate.
Regional or multilateral agreements are also used to manage cross-border migration flows. These agreements are legally binding and form part of the international legal order. While some of these agreements are more co-operative in nature, others can be compulsory. Regional or multilateral agreements are also commonly used to manage the issue of irregular migration. For instance, most of the agreements used to manage irregular migration flows in the Mediterranean are regional in nature.
Institutional arrangements are often used to manage migration flows through the coordination of the activities of existing international organizations. For instance, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) assists with the resettlement of refugees through the use of multilateral agreements and bilateral resettlement arrangements.

​Most governments and law enforcement agencies have some kind of “use-of-force” policy that governs the degree to which police or other security services are allowed to use force to make an arrest or stop a suspect. Such policies are used to ensure that the use of force is limited to the point where there is a clear and immediate threat to life and limb. Such policies usually also lay out the circumstances in which use of force may be necessary.
However, asylum seekers have no right to be in a country, so such policies are not typically applicable. In fact, the status of an asylum seeker makes his or her status ambiguous, and therefore not governed by the same rules that apply to citizens or residents.
Therefore, when an asylum seeker is picked up by the police or security services, the question of whether force may be used to arrest the person is clouded by the fact that he or she is not a citizen or a permanent resident. The police are under no obligation to follow the same policies that govern the use of force against citizens and residents.
Governments that are reluctant to hand over their asylum seekers to law enforcement authorities, or to make laws that govern the treatment of asylum seekers by the police, should avoid allowing their asylum systems to be used by those who are actually undesirable, such as terrorists or drug traffickers.

The Global Forum on Migration and Development (GFMD) is an intergovernmental policy forum held annually to provide governments with an opportunity to exchange practices, experiences, and best policies on migration and development. It was established in 2007 at the initiative of the United Nations Secretary-General, and is supported by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the International Labour Organization (ILO). It operates under the leadership of the Secretary-General, and governments participate on the basis of equality, mutual respect, and a sense of common purpose. Its main objective is to bring governments together with key stakeholders to exchange views, experiences, and best practices on policies, processes, and actions related to international migration and development. Each year, the GFMD provides an opportunity to review progress made in achieving this objective, and to reflect on the way forward.
The GFMD has two main components: (i) a plenary session, and (ii) a series of regional consultations and thematic meetings.
The plenary session brings together Member States, civil society organizations, and international and regional organizations, to review progress and identify challenges related to international migration and development. The meeting is organized into six working groups, focusing on different themes and issues related to migration and development, and each with a different theme, as follows:
1. Protection, Mobility, and Development
2. Governance, Partnerships, and Economic Development
3. Movements, People-to-People, and Regional Interactions
4. Youth and Migration
5. Gender, Diversity, and Migration
6. Human Rights, Security, and Migration
A series of regional consultations and thematic meetings are also held in the lead up to the plenary session.

Those most likely to say that technology and data analytics have led to a major increase in law enforcement effectiveness are younger (47% of those under 45 vs. 29% of those 45 and older), more male (48% vs. 29%), and of non-Hispanic white ethnicity (48% vs. 32%).

2011-14 was the third highest recorded wave of immigration into the United States, with 38 million foreign-born individuals in the United States, accounting for 13% of the U.S. population. Twenty percent of U.S. residents speak a language other than English in their homes. Language barriers can be a significant obstacle to communication between government and community, making it difficult for new residents to access the services and information they need.
Governments have several options for addressing language barriers. For example, several U.S. cities, such as San Francisco and Chicago, have created government-run multilingual services to better meet the needs of the increasingly diverse populations they serve. Some cities, such as Denver and Austin, have outsourced multilingual services to private companies to ensure that government services are available in as many languages as needed. In addition, some local governments provide multilingual services on their own, often using a model that allows residents to call a toll-free number to reach an interpreter who can communicate with government officials.
In the U.S. states, a growing number of state governments are required to offer services in languages other than English. For example, Maine, Massachusetts, and New Jersey each offer services to the deaf and hard-of-hearing in American Sign Language and Spanish and offer translation services for limited English proficiency (LEP) residents. Several U.S. cities, such as Denver, Colorado Springs, and Chicago, have enacted language access laws to ensure that government services are accessible to LEP populations.
In Canada, most government services are offered in English and French, but there are some exceptions. For example, the Canadian government offers many services in 11 Indigenous languages and has implemented sign language interpreters for deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals.
Government workers are often unsure of how to address language barriers and are often limited in their ability to serve non-English-speaking constituents. This is a challenge not only for government services, but for the governments themselves. For example, Denver has observed a sharp decrease in citizen participation in public meetings since outsourcing the city’s multilingual services.
Participants at a workshop on language access held by the International City/County Management Association.
Language barriers can be particularly challenging for local governments, which must often serve communities that speak a variety of languages and dialects. For example, in some cities in the United States, Chinese speakers may be clustered in particular neighborhoods, while Russian speakers may live in the same neighborhood but not speak Chinese. In other cities, only a small percentage of residents speak English as their primary language.
As more migrants arrive in cities and states, local governments will have to decide how to meet the needs of increasingly diverse populations. Government officials and administrators should consider whether to address language barriers through a centralized service, a local outsourcing model, or a hybrid approach. Local governments also need to ensure that their employees are trained to effectively serve diverse populations.

Q: How does MITRE assist law enforcement with conducting investigations?
A: MITRE develops and deploys tools to assist law enforcement. There is a whole suite of forensic tools that MITRE has developed to help law enforcement look at the evidence, recover data, and present it in court.

We also help them understand how to conduct an investigation, such as which tools to use, where to look and how to analyze the evidence that they have recovered.
For example, one of our tools is called FileFixation, which is designed to analyze a suspect’s computer, and identify which pieces of data are associated with the particular crime that they are investigating.
Q: What are some examples of the types of cybercrime that MITRE works with law enforcement to investigate?
A: The criminals that we see are most often involved in extortion, blackmail or fraud. They will often target a company and extort the company into paying a ransom in Bitcoin, or they will steal confidential information and hold that information for ransom.
Criminals will also target small businesses by infecting their computers with ransomware, and extorting them into paying the ransom by encrypting all of their files and threatening to destroy the files.
Q: Is it possible for victims to recover their data without paying the ransom?
A: Yes, there is a process where the victims can go to a third party who has the capability to decrypt the files and recover the data without paying the ransom. Lastly, it is important for businesses to understand how to protect themselves from a ransomware attack. This means regularly updating your operating system, and installing software updates as they are released.

Charter, which is ratified by every member state, sets out the basic principles of international relations. Article 55 of the Charter provides for the promotion of human rights, which is then carried out by the U.N.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which was approved by the U.N. General Assembly in 1948, sets out the basic rights and freedoms that are to be enjoyed by everyone. It is not legally binding, but states have accepted the obligations that it imposes. The UDHR is a major source of inspiration for international human rights law. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) were subsequently adopted by the U.N. General Assembly, setting out rights in more detail. The ICCPR and the ICESCR are legally binding on states that have ratified them. There are now 169 states that have ratified the ICCPR, and 166 that have ratified the ICESCR.
Both the ICCPR and the ICESCR have been incorporated into domestic law in most states. Although they are not directly applicable to non-state actors, individuals can make claims under them if they can show that a state is violating them by failing to prevent a private actor from violating them.
The Refugee Convention, which has been ratified by 149 states, and the Convention against Torture, which has been ratified by 156 states, are legally binding on those states.
The Human Rights Committee, which is an independent body set up under the ICCPR, monitors compliance with the treaty. Individuals can bring complaints about violations of the treaty to the Committee. The Committee is composed of 18 independent experts who are elected by the U.N. General Assembly for a four-year term. The Committee’s decisions are legally binding on the state that is being complained about.
The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) is an important treaty that applies to all European states. It has been incorporated into domestic law in all but three states, which are not members of the Council of Europe. The ECHR is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), which is an international court. Individuals can bring complaints about violations of the ECHR to the ECtHR. The ECtHR is composed of 70 judges, who are elected by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. Their decisions are legally binding on the state that is being complained about.

While the U.S. is not a party to the Refugee Convention, the U.S. allows refugee status to be granted to individuals who meet the criteria of the Refugee Convention and are considered to be at risk if they return to their home country.
The U.S. has ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW). This treaty obliges the U.S. to ensure the fundamental rights of women. CEDAW is legally binding on the U.S.
The U.S. has ratified the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. This treaty requires the U.S. to protect the rights of migrant workers and their families and to provide them with access to equal treatment and justice.

Q: What are the characteristics of a private prison?
A: Private prisons are for-profit facilities that house immigrants in detention, and are contracted by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). For-profit private prisons share the same goals as private security companies.
Q: How do private prisons benefit from the incarceration of immigrants?
A: Private prisons benefit from the incarceration of immigrants in multiple ways.​
Q: What is the difference between local and federal law enforcement?
A: Local law enforcement agencies do not have the power or authority to enforce federal immigration law. Local law enforcement cannot detain someone solely on the basis of an immigration detainer, or request that someone be detained because of suspected immigration violations. If a local law enforcement agency has a detainer, they are required to notify the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of any detention. Local law enforcement officers, like all other federal, state, and local law enforcement officers, are prohibited from asking people about their immigration status or legal status.
Q: What happens when ICE arrests someone?
A: When ICE arrests someone, they enter the person's information into their records system. ICE then gives the person a document called the ICE Detainer, which is a written request for that person to be held for up to 48 hours past their scheduled release time.
Q: What does ICE use to determine whether someone is "criminal alien"?
A: ICE uses the Priority Enforcement Program (PEP) as the criteria for whom they arrest and detain.​
Q: What are the PEPs?
A: Under the Priority Enforcement Program (PEP), ICE prioritizes their investigations and arrests of immigrants to focus on detaining individuals who are:
Fugitives from immigration court.
Unlawfully present in the U.S. for more than two years.
Unlawfully present in the U.S. for more than one year and convicted of a crime.

Using biometric technology (fingerprints and/or facial recognition) to verify identity.
Verifying identity through other means such as biographical data, confirmation of identity from other governments or agencies, or an interview with the applicant.
Verifying identity through a combination of biometric technology and interviews.
Using secure storage units for documents and biometric data, and only allowing access to appropriate officials.

A: Examples of ways governments are improving their procedures to address document fraud include:
Making sure that the applicant is interviewed at the earliest possible point in the procedure and at all times ensuring that the asylum seeker is not subjected to unnecessary detention.
Ensuring that documents are stored securely and only available to the asylum seeker, the government official reviewing the application and only as required by the asylum seeker or government official.
Requiring that the asylum seeker or an authorized representative be present during the interview to review the application to ensure that they are the ones submitting the application and that the information is accurate.
Having the asylum seeker sign a statement acknowledging that he/she is the person submitting the application and that the information is true and accurate.
Requiring that the asylum seeker or authorized representative sign an affidavit stating that he/she has not misrepresented any information in the application.

17 international instruments and a growing body of national laws recognize the right of individuals to migrate. States have a duty to facilitate orderly, safe, and legal migration and to protect the human rights of all migrants regardless of their migratory status. The right of individuals to migrate and the duty of states to protect those rights are complementary rather than competing.
Both can be strengthened through cooperation between states and through diplomatic negotiations.
This process begins with an exchange of information between the sending and receiving states on the national systems in place for the protection of migrants’ rights, as well as the level of cooperation between states on migration issues.
It also involves making arrangements for the exchange of information on individual cases, such as individuals who have been forcibly returned.
These arrangements must be negotiated between the parties in good faith.
If the parties are not able to reach agreement, they should submit the matter to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for adjudication.
The ICJ has the legal authority to rule on cases involving state responsibilities under the UN Charter and international law.
It has also ruled on matters of state responsibility for migrant deaths, including the 1983 ruling on the case of the sinking of the Bolivian Navy vessel “Santa Cruz,” which resulted in 28 Colombian migrants drowning.
The ICJ’s 1991 ruling on the Bangladesh-Myanmar maritime boundary dispute is relevant to the issue of migrants’ rights.
In the case, the ICJ ruled that, under international law, Myanmar should not restrict the movements of Bangladeshi migrants across its borders.
Myanmar’s obligations to protect the human rights of migrants and to facilitate their legal and orderly migration were the same as its obligations to other migrants.
The ICJ’s ruling in the case of the “Santa Cruz” demonstrates that the State has a legal duty to ensure the protection of migrants against violations of their rights.
The ruling also demonstrates the importance of cooperation between states and states’ commitment to facilitating safe and legal migration.

Countries began to engage with one another on migration issues through cooperation and dialogue, which involved information exchange and joint efforts to address migration challenges.
This approach has evolved into the current regional consultative process on migration, which aims to develop a regional approach to migration and to facilitate the protection and promotion of migrants’ rights.
Regional cooperation has been particularly important in North America.
Since the signing of the 1994 Agreement between the United States and Mexico, the United States has been working to build a secure, orderly, and humane system of migration.
This is a policy of engagement and dialogue that aims to promote the effective management of international migration and to protect the human rights of migrants.
Engagement and dialogue between the United States and Mexico on migration issues has been ongoing since 1994.
Both countries have signed a number of bilateral agreements and memoranda of understanding (MOUs) to foster cooperation on migration.
They have also worked together to implement a number of migration-related projects and initiatives.
One example is the Mérida Initiative, which aims to support the Mexican government’s efforts to improve the rule of law, particularly in regards to the control of the southern border.
Another example is the United States-Mexico Border Governance Initiative, which seeks to improve the coordination of border activities between the United States and Mexico in the areas of border management, cross-border trade, and migration.
Since 2005, the United States has also been working with Canada and Mexico on the Security and Prosperity Partnership (SPP).
The SPP aims to increase cooperation and coordination between the United States, Canada, and Mexico on security and economic issues, including migration.
The SPP also promotes the efficient and secure movement of people, goods, and services across the Canada-United States and Mexico-United States borders.

12 March 2017, Source: Daily Monitor, Sam Okwojj, THE United Nations refugee agency has said that governments in the Horn of Africa should come up with effective and innovative policies to address the challenges related to human smuggling via maritime routes.
Human smuggling through the maritime routes in the region is on the rise as migrants from the Horn of Africa continue to use boats to reach their preferred destinations in Europe.
Nebiat Binyam, acting head of UNHCR’s Puntland sub-office, says they are dealing with smuggling through different forms including boats, aircraft, and even riding on trucks.
He says, however, that the most common are boats and airplanes. “We are seeing these cases in different ways; we are seeing smuggling by sea, smuggling by air and smuggling by land,” says Mr Binyam.
He says the smuggling activities started in 2008 with the increase in the number of arrivals to Europe from the Horn of Africa.
Binyam says there has been a huge increase in the number of refugees coming to the region and hence the need for the government to devise new and innovative ways to deal with the challenge.
UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, is the lead agency in the region dealing with the challenges of human smuggling.
It is one of the organisations working with other government agencies and civil society organisations on the issue.
“If you look at the situation in the region, we have two major problems; one is the arrival of refugees from the region to Europe, and the other one is the arrival of refugees from the region to the United States and Canada,” Binyam says.
“If you look at the situation, 2014 was the peak of arrivals, and the main reason was the increase in the number of refugees to Europe.
He says they have been working with the government to address the challenges but the response so far has been very slow.
Binyam says, however, that the government is now putting in place some mechanisms, including relocating the refugees to other countries and the establishment of camps for refugees in the region.
He says the government has established camps in Puntland, including a camp in Shiilka, and another camp in Bossaso.
However, Binyam says the camps are not yet functional because of the lack of resources to run them.
“These are camps, but they are not functional yet,” Binyam says.
He says the government is still working on the policies on the issue, which he says could take long.
Binyam says they are also providing capacity building to different government departments, including the ministry of justice and public safety.
He says the ministry of justice is now working on a national refugee action plan. “The ministry of justice and public safety are working on a national refugee action plan,” Binyam says.
“We have seen the idea of the national refugee action plan in some of the neighbouring countries such as Kenya and Uganda.
“We hope this idea will be replicated in Puntland.
“What we are seeing now is that countries are developing national refugee action plans.
“These plans are also based on the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework, which is a UNHCR idea for providing a comprehensive response for refugees and their host communities.
“A national refugee action plan is a good way to deal with the challenge and to provide protection to refugees and to their host communities.
“Hence, UNHCR will continue to work with the government to implement this idea.
“UNHCR is working with governments to deal with the challenge of human smuggling.
“We are also working with governments to develop a mechanism to share the costs and responsibilities of refugees, and to provide protection to refugees and host communities.

A migrant worker has the same right to just and favourable conditions of work as nationals. This includes access to health care, social security, maternity leave, annual leave, termination of the contract of employment and retirement. The right to just and favourable conditions of work is often affected by the type of contract used. In many cases, migrant workers are employed on temporary contracts, but these do not provide them with the same protection as permanent contracts. Contracts of the first type give the employer the right to terminate the contract for a reason other than serious misconduct. Contracts of the second type give the employer the right to terminate the contract only in the case of serious misconduct. Employers should ensure that migrant workers receive, at least, the same conditions of work as national workers.

A migrant worker is entitled to the protection of the law, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status. The State should make sure that no law, regulation or administrative provision discriminates against migrant workers.

Migrant workers have the right to equal rights and treatment as compared to nationals, as long as they are legally staying in the country. States should make sure that migrant workers enjoy equal rights and treatment as nationals, unless they are granted preferential treatment by law.

A migrant worker has the right to join an association of migrant workers or to form trade unions to protect and promote his or her interests. A migrant worker also has the right to form trade unions, as long as they are not engaged in illegal activities or seek to overthrow the government.

28 countries that were part of the EU-3 (Austria, France, Germany) and 18 EU-15 (Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden) shared their experiences with asylum seekers who have a past criminal record in a report that was published by the European Commission on 23 May 2012.
The report, 'Finding a way forward: Adjudicating applications from asylum seekers with a criminal record', looks at how EU governments have dealt with asylum seekers with a past criminal record and the policies they have adopted in this regard.
According to the report, the Dublin regulation requires that asylum seekers are examined in the first safe country of arrival in the EU.
While the vast majority of asylum seekers with a past criminal record were recognised as refugees in 2009, the report finds that there is a high level of variation in the way EU governments have dealt with this issue.
The report highlights that almost half of the EU-3 and 37% of the EU-15 governments acknowledge that they have no or little information on asylum seekers with a past criminal record.
The Dublin regulation also requires that asylum seekers who are found to have a past criminal record are returned to the first country where they are identified as having a criminal record.
The report notes that the same large variation in practices between EU governments is also found in the area of returns.
The report points out that almost 70% of the respondents (EU-3 and EU-15) have adopted or plan to adopt a policy to screen all asylum seekers for a past criminal record, regardless of the country of origin.
However, the report stresses that the screening of applicants for a past criminal record is a long process. It needs to be done in a structured way in order to avoid that all asylum seekers are screened for a past criminal record, regardless of their country of origin.
The report suggests that a system of suspended returns or a specific set of circumstances when a return is suspended should be established.
The report also suggests that governments should look at how to cooperate in order to exchange information on past criminal record, including extradition.
The report stresses that EU governments need to adapt their practices in order to ensure that they comply with the EU and international law.

1. The police are in the frontline of the fight against corruption. They are often the primary point of contact with the public and have a special position in society, which makes them vulnerable to corruption. Given the power they have, they can easily take advantage of their position by pressuring those who seek their assistance. The police can be corrupted by private individuals, who they have reason to protect. They can be corrupted by organized criminals who they are entrusted to investigate. And they can be corrupted by their colleagues, who may offer them a bribe in exchange for looking the other way or for aiding them in a criminal activity. One of the main issues is that corruption is not easily detectable. This is especially true in instances where the police are corrupt but do not abuse their power or their position. This can be seen in the immigration context where police officers are complicit in illegal immigration and in the trafficking of human beings. If they are not caught, the corruption goes unpunished and continues. Corruption can be detected and avoided in a number of ways. First of all, the police need to be made aware that corruption exists and that it is a crime that will not be tolerated. This can be done by educating officers on the legal prohibition of corruption. Secondly, the police need to develop a code of ethics that outlines what is and is not acceptable behavior. If a police officer or other employee of the police is corrupt, there needs to be a mechanism to detect and punish corruption, such as an internal affairs unit. The police and any other employees who come in contact with the public, including those who work in administrative and support roles, need to have their conduct monitored in order to ensure that they are not abusing their position or the trust placed in them by the public. Thirdly, the police need to be provided with mechanisms to avoid corruption. For example, a police officer should not be able to take a bribe unless it is done in the presence of another officer. The police need to ensure that they have control over their surroundings. The police need to be honest with the public in order to earn their trust and avoid corruption. The public need to be aware of their rights and should not feel intimidated by the police. The police need to be held accountable for their actions, including their use of discretion. This can be done through random spot checks of officers and through the use of independent oversight committees or commissions. In a large police department, the use of specialized units to deal with particular crimes, such as organized crime, may reduce the likelihood of corruption. It may also be possible to reduce the risk of corruption by having the same officer work on the same file from start to finish. This would ensure that the officer was not in a position to abuse his or her discretion by changing the facts of a file in order to benefit a friend, a relative or a colleague. All of this may seem obvious, but it is important to remember that corruption is still a significant problem. In many countries, corruption is endemic and it is widespread within the police. In 2009, Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index ranked the police in 70 out of 178 countries on a scale of one to ten, where 10 represented the least corrupt and 1 represented the most corrupt. The police in 44 countries were ranked as being highly corrupt, whereas 25 countries were ranked as being corrupt, 9 countries as being somewhat corrupt and 3 countries as being not corrupt. This puts the police in a position that allows them to exercise discretion on a daily basis. The fact that this discretion is abused indicates that the police are not being held accountable for their actions. This is even more troubling in the immigration context, where the police are entrusted to carry out the law of the land. When they abuse their power and discretion, they are engaging in an act of disobedience, which may even be criminal. As well, when police officers abuse their power, it often undermines the public’s trust in the police, which can have a detrimental effect on the success of law enforcement.

178 countries worldwide have signed and ratified the 1951 UN Convention relating to the Status of Refugees. The Convention sets out the definition of a refugee and the obligations of countries to provide refuge to them. In addition, refugees are protected by a series of international conventions and protocols such as the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees and the 1969 Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa.
A large number of asylum seekers are not refugees but rather economic migrants. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has developed a manual to assist governments to determine the status of asylum seekers. In particular, UNHCR outlines a series of questions to be asked to help asylum seekers establish their status.
For countries that are party to the 1951 UN Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, asylum seekers who have entered the country on a valid visa are generally treated as refugees. Some countries, such as Australia, have a sophisticated identification system for refugees. This system allows for the assessment of claims made by asylum seekers before they enter the country, and any asylum seekers found not to be refugees are returned to their country of origin.
Other countries assess asylum seekers’ claims after they have entered the country and asylum seekers are detained in camps. These countries do not have an efficient identification system for refugees. For example, in Niger, there is a UNHCR camp that holds 80,000 refugees. This is an extremely high number for a country with a population of 15 million. Countries that do not have an efficient identification system for refugees are called ‘refugee diasporas’.
In some cases, a country may have a very high level of human rights abuses, including genocide and political oppression. In these cases, asylum seekers may not have a valid visa to enter the country. For example, in 1994, the Rwandan government, after an extremely brutal civil war, refused to accept all Rwandan refugees. Some countries, including Canada, resettled a large number of Rwandan refugees.
Governments may decide to bring a group of asylum seekers back to their country of origin. This is called repatriation. It is usually done when there is an agreement between the country of origin and the receiving country. In most cases, this agreement is written into a bilateral treaty. The asylum seekers are usually detained in a camp while their status is being determined.
Most countries send their nationals back to their country of origin, unless they are genuine refugees. For example, Australia returns its citizens to Australia. However, some countries, including Canada, do not repatriate its citizens.
There are many issues that affect the ability of governments to return failed asylum seekers. In particular, there are issues related to human rights and political oppression in the country of origin.
In some countries, it is too dangerous for returned asylum seekers to return to their home country. For example, in Afghanistan, the Taliban has a policy of executing people who are of the minority ethnic group, the Hazara.
Some countries may have too many asylum seekers. For example, Australia has a limited number of refugees that they will accept. This is why there are 11,000 refugees on Nauru. These people are in a very difficult situation.
There are a number of laws and agreements that regulate the return of failed asylum seekers. For example, the UN Refugee Convention and the Geneva Convention set out the rights of refugees. The Refugee Convention has been signed by all countries in the world except for the United States of America. The Refugee Convention sets out the rights of refugees including the right of refugees to an efficient identification system for refugees.
There are also regional agreements such as the African Union Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and the European Convention on Human Rights. Both of these agreements set out the rights of refugees and the rights of asylum seekers.
The Refugee Convention and the Geneva Convention set out the rights of refugees. These agreements are the cornerstone of international refugee law.

1. The UK Immigration and Nationality Directorate (IND) (now part of the Home Office) is responsible for the assessment of immigration policy. The IND uses a range of indicators to measure social cohesion, which includes immigration and its impacts. This is done via a number of government sponsored research projects. The Home Office has also developed a set of indicators to assess the impact of immigration on social cohesion. A research unit is also engaged in on-going research projects on the impact of immigration on the economy, housing, crime and social cohesion.
2. The Commission on Integration and Cohesion in the UK (CIC) is an independent body, established by the government to produce an annual report on integration in the UK. It does this by monitoring relevant government policies and investigating issues relating to integration. The CIC defines social cohesion in the following way: "Social cohesion is the result of successful integration. It is about the degree to which people from different backgrounds are able to form and maintain relationships and to interact with each other in the shared spaces and places of daily life. It is about the degree to which they trust each other and respect each other's culture, background and traditions". The CIC uses the following indicators to measure integration and social cohesion:
Economic and Social status: data on income, housing, poverty, unemployment, education, health etc.
Political participation: data on voting behaviour, political affiliation and general attitudes and beliefs
Housing: data on ownership, population density, ethnicity etc
Crime: data on ethnicity of victims and perpetrators, racial harassment and racially motivated crime, etc.
Employment: data on levels of unemployment, ethnic differences in employment, etc.
Ethnicity: data on ethnicity, in particular, the White British population, White British and Irish population, ethnic minority populations etc.
Civic participation: data on levels of volunteering, donations, etc.
Language: data on linguistic skills, use of languages in the workplace, etc.
Religion: data on religious affiliation, prayer, worship etc.
Family and kinship: data on marital status, divorce, cohabitation etc.
Sexual behaviour: data on sexual orientation, STI etc.
Attitudes: data on attitudes towards the EU, immigration, ethnic minorities, etc.
All the data is obtained from official sources, eg, from the Office of National Statistics (ONS) and the Department for Communities and Local Government (DCLG).

2005 was the International Year of Microcredit and civil society organizations were very active in advocating for migrant rights. We organized a national forum on migration in November 2005 where civil society organizations came together with public officials from different institutions to discuss migrant rights. The main objective of the forum was to evaluate the response of the state in the protection of migrants’ rights.
During the forum, we also came up with a national action plan which is still valid for the next three years. It was very important for us because it brought together various stakeholders who could participate in advocating for migrants.
Civil society organizations play a very important role in advocating for migrant rights. This is because the majority of migrants are not aware of their rights and are very vulnerable. So the role of civil society organizations is very important to raise awareness and protect migrants.
Read more about Q: What role do civil society organizations play in advocating for migrant rights?
Q: How do you carry out your work in a country that does not respect migrant rights?
A: The lack of respect for migrants is a problem, but it is not an obstacle for our work. We are very persistent in our advocacy work and have succeeded in changing attitudes.
For example, before we organized the 2005 forum on migrants, there were few or no discussions about migrants in the country. When we organized that forum, many public officials were interested in participating and learnt about migrants’ rights. Since then, there has been more discussion about migrants in the media, which has helped change attitudes in the country.
Q: What is the situation of migrants in Mauritania?
A: 80% of Mauritanians are not aware of migrants’ rights and 85% of migrants do not know their rights. The majority of migrants are also illiterate and are not aware of their rights.
Most migrants go to Algeria, Morocco or Libya. When they get there, they are sold and forced into slavery. The families they left behind do not know what has happened to them. These migrants are very vulnerable and are sometimes sold and abused and sometimes they are sent back to Mauritania to face the police and prosecutors. They are often put in jail and sometimes killed.
Q: How can a country become more tolerant to migrants and make them feel like citizens?
A: One of the most important strategies to improve the situation of migrants is through education. Education must focus on respect and inclusion. We have to accept migrants as a positive force for the country.
The Mauritanian authorities also need to organize a public debate and discuss the situation of migrants. We also need to work on a national action plan on migration. All this would help improve the situation of migrants.

1.	The European Union (EU) is an important and powerful player in global governance and decision-making. The EU is the largest aid donor in the world, and also the world’s largest trading bloc. As such, its influence is hugely significant. This means that when the EU makes human rights declarations and agreements, it sets an example that other states, including Ireland, will follow.
2.	The EU is signatory to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Both of these instruments contain anti-discrimination provisions, which encompass LGBTQ+ individuals. In 2017, the EU adopted a set of EU Guidelines on the rights of LGBTI people. While the Guidelines are non-binding, they are a valuable tool in influencing policy change in EU Member States.
3.	The European Commission has recently appointed a new EU Coordinator for Combatting Anti-Semitism, Racism and Xenophobia. This role has not previously been filled, and the appointment of this new Coordinator is a positive step towards tackling rising anti-Semitism in the EU. I am concerned that racism, xenophobia and homophobia are on the increase, and that the new Coordinator’s work will be relevant to LGBTQ+ asylum seekers.
4.	The European Union (EU) has adopted the Code of Conduct on the Common European Asylum System (CEAS). The CEAS is a set of common rules and standards for asylum and refugee procedures that member states must implement. The CEAS is in effect across the EU, and each country is obliged to implement the same common standards and procedures.
5.	However, Ireland is not fully compliant with the Code of Conduct, and in some respects is lagging behind. For example, Ireland does not provide sufficient legal protection for LGBTQ+ individuals to make a claim for asylum, as they are not included in the Refugee Act 2016. This means that LGBTQ+ individuals in Ireland are not legally protected in the same way as those who are persecuted on the grounds of race, religion, nationality or membership of the travelling community.
6.	In addition, Ireland has not ratified the Council of Europe’s Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. This convention has an important safeguard provision, article 12, which states that a woman who is forced to leave her country due to domestic violence will not be penalised for doing so. This means that Ireland is not fulfilling its obligations under international law to protect women fleeing domestic violence.
7.	Furthermore, the EU-Mid-term review, published in November 2018, notes that Ireland has not made sufficient progress in the area of legal migration. The report states that Ireland has not taken any action to ensure that the right to family reunification is fully respected, and that the Irish Government must take action to rectify this situation.
8.	I have raised my concerns about the failure of the Irish Government to implement the recommendations of the EU Mid-term review on legal migration in the Seanad on a number of occasions, and I have asked the Minister for Justice and Equality to address these concerns in a timely fashion.
9.	I have also raised my concerns about the lack of legal protections for LGBTQ+ individuals with the Minister for Justice and Equality on several occasions. 2015 has been a year of record-breaking refugee movements, with over 60 million displaced worldwide. The challenge of accommodating refugees and their children has become a global priority and this issue has been repeatedly brought to the forefront of national and international policy agendas. We know that education can mitigate the risks faced by vulnerable children and protect them from exploitation and abuse. Many countries have made significant efforts to develop a national education strategy to address the needs of refugee children and the situation varies widely.
In this podcast, we speak with Dr. Tom Carnoy, Director of the Center for International Education at Stanford University and Chair of the Education Working Group of UNHCR’s Global Consultations on Refugee Protection and Solutions. Dr. Carnoy’s recent report, “Education of refugee children in crisis situations: A global review”, presents the findings of a two-year review of the global status of the education of refugee children and youth in crisis situations. The report includes a chapter on “Integration of refugee children into national education systems”. The report also includes recommendations to governments, national and local education authorities and agencies that deliver education to refugees and other vulnerable children.

Tom Carnoy, Ph.D., is a Distinguished Research Professor in the School of Education at Stanford University, where he also directs the Center for International Education. He is the author of numerous books and articles on the issues of education in developing countries, with a special focus on post-conflict and fragile states. He has worked with governments and international agencies in over 50 countries and was the first Chief Technical Advisor for the Global Partnership for Education. He has received numerous awards for his work, including a MacArthur Fellowship.
The UNHCR Global Consultations on Refugee Protection and Solutions is a series of consultations that have taken place since 2009. This series of consultations is part of an ongoing commitment to ensure that UNHCR’s work to protect and assist refugees is informed by a broad and diverse range of voices, perspectives and experiences. The Consultations have brought together key stakeholders from civil society, the private sector, national and international governmental agencies, the UN system and international organizations, research institutions and the media.
The report is available in English, French, Arabic, Spanish, and Farsi.
